The agreement states basic services, additional services, rates, payment terms, 60 days' written notice of rate changes, refund conditions, preadmission fee limits and refunds, the visiting policy, the firearms policy, the grievance procedure, eviction grounds and notice rights, the Department's authority to examine resident records, and the right to contact CDSS and the Ombudsman. The agreement contains no liability waivers or other prohibited provisions.

definitions.definition: The individual written contract between the facility and the resident or representative under 22 CCR §87507.
A single fee that may be charged once per admission, must be refundable, and must be described in writing.
The services included in the base rate.
Optional services that cost extra and are listed with their rates in the agreement.
The Telecommunications Device Notification form for residents with a hearing or other disability.

procedures: The Licensee prepares the admission agreement template in 12-point black type on plain white paper, one-sided, in plain language, with titled sections. The Administrator checks it against §87507 and has it reviewed by [ATTORNEY OR CONSULTANT NAME] before use.

The agreement lists basic services, additional services and their rates, payment terms, the visiting policy, the firearms policy, the grievance procedure, the grounds for eviction and the notice and appeal rights, the Department's authority to examine resident records, and the right to contact CDSS and the Ombudsman.

The agreement does not contain any liability waiver, release of the facility from negligence, or other provision §87507(h) prohibits. The Administrator removes any such wording before the agreement is offered.
Blank copies of the agreement are given to the public on request, with copying fees at cost. A copy, or a notice that copies are available, is posted in the facility.

Before signing, the Administrator reviews the agreement with the applicant and representative, answers questions, and gives them time to read it. Translation or interpretation is arranged when needed (see RR-08).

If the pre-admission appraisal shows the resident has a hearing or other disability, the Administrator completes LIC 9158 Telecommunications Device Notification and places it in the resident file (see ADM-01).

Only one preadmission fee may be charged per admission. It is refundable and described in writing. The facility does not charge a preadmission fee or deposit to any SSI/SSP recipient, and does not charge any damage deposit.

If a preadmission fee is paid, the Administrator refunds 100% if the applicant decides not to enter before the preadmission appraisal, or if the required disclosure was not made. For fees above $500, the refund is at least 80% of the excess if the applicant leaves in month 1, 60% in month 2, and 40% in month 3.

The resident or representative and the licensee (or [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] as designee) sign and date the agreement within 7 days of admission. A copy is handed to the resident or representative immediately. The original and all modifications are kept in the resident file (see REC-01).
If the payor is a different person from the representative, the Administrator also gives written notice and copies of rate and refund terms to the payor.

The Administrator gives at least 60 days' written notice of any change to a rate or rate structure, or notice as soon as the facility is told of a change in SSI/SSP payment. Rate changes follow the conditions in the Health and Safety Code as referenced in §87507. The notice and proof of delivery are kept in the resident file.
Any change to services or terms is made as a written, signed modification to the agreement. No change takes effect without notice to the resident or representative.

When a resident leaves, the Administrator calculates a refund of prepaid fees as a proportional daily amount. If the resident gave 5 days' notice, the refund is paid at move-out. Otherwise it is paid within 7 days of the resident vacating. A written accounting accompanies the refund.

When a resident dies, the Administrator refunds advance monthly fees as required by the death-refund provisions referenced in §87507(g)(5)(A), and sends a written notice and accounting to the payor and the person responsible.
The Administrator reviews 100% of new agreements within 7 days of admission using the Agreement Checklist, and reviews the agreement template yearly or whenever the regulations change (see GOV-04).

The Administrator keeps copies of all rate-change notices, refund calculations and payments in the resident file, and reports any billing errors to the Licensee for correction within 5 business days (see GOV-06).

responsibilities.duty: Approves the agreement template and rates, signs each agreement, and approves refunds.
Explains and completes the agreement, gives copies, gives 60-day rate notices, calculates and pays refunds, and files records.
Prepare agreements and billing under the Administrator's direction and keep fee records accurate.

documentation: Signed and dated admission agreement and all modifications in the resident file
LIC 9158 where applicable
Preadmission fee receipt and refund records
60-day rate change notices with proof of delivery
Refund calculations, accountings and payment records
Agreement Checklist and template review record

policies.title: Resident Funds, Personal Property, Valuables, and Theft and Loss
policies.applies_to: All staff, residents, residents' representatives, and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To protect each resident's money, personal property and valuables, to honor the resident's right to keep and spend his or her own money, and to ensure that any reported theft or loss is promptly addressed, investigated and documented.
policies.policy: Residents of [AGENCY NAME] have the right to keep and spend their own money and to keep personal possessions (22 CCR §87468.1). The facility will never withhold a resident's money as punishment or as leverage in any dispute. The Administrator decides, before licensure and in writing, whether the facility will hold resident cash. If the facility does hold resident cash, it will comply with 22 CCR §87217: LIC 400 affidavit, LIC 402 surety bond, a receipt for every transaction, accounting records, and a separate account titled as the residents' money with no commingling with facility funds. If the facility does not hold resident cash, staff will not accept it, and residents will be helped to arrange safekeeping through a family member, representative or financial institution. The facility's written theft and loss policy (LIC 281 attachment B14) is set out in the procedures below.

definitions.definition: Money belonging to a resident that is entrusted to the facility for safekeeping or spending.
Mixing resident money with facility operating funds or with another resident's money in a way that prevents separate accounting.
Items of significant monetary or sentimental value, such as jewelry, cash, checks, important papers, electronics and hearing aids.
Any report or discovery that a resident's money or property is missing, damaged or taken without the resident's consent.

procedures: Before the license application is filed, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] records in the Plan of Operation (GOV-04) whether the facility will or will not hold resident cash. The admission agreement (RR-04) states the decision.

If the facility will hold cash, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] completes and files the LIC 400 affidavit and obtains the LIC 402 surety bond before any resident cash is accepted. Copies are kept in the administrative file.
The facility opens a separate account titled as the residents' money. No facility funds, owner funds or staff funds are deposited in it, and it is never used for operating expenses.

The Administrator or a designated staff member obtains the resident's (or representative's) written authorization before accepting any cash. Staff issue a dated, signed receipt for each deposit or withdrawal, and the resident or representative gets a copy.

Staff keep an individual ledger for each resident showing date, amount, purpose, balance and the signatures of the resident (or representative) and the staff member. Entries are made the same day as the transaction.

Funds held are counted and reconciled to the individual ledgers and the account balance at least monthly by someone other than the person who made most of the entries. The reconciliation is signed and dated by [ADMINISTRATOR NAME].

A statement of the resident's account is offered to the resident and representative at least monthly, and at any time on request. Funds are returned promptly on request and at discharge, with a final accounting and signed receipt.

Staff never borrow from, loan to, accept gifts of money from, or use the funds or property of any resident (see STF-06). Residents' funds are never withheld as punishment or for any disciplinary reason.

At admission, staff offer to prepare an inventory of the resident's personal property and valuables, signed by the resident or representative and a staff member. Staff update it when items are added or removed.

Residents are told they may keep valuables in a lockable space in their room, and the facility offers a secure storage option for valuables where available. Staff explain that the facility's liability limits cannot be waived in the admission agreement.

Any resident, representative, staff member or visitor may report a theft or loss to any staff member, to [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], or through the grievance process (RR-02). Staff accept every report without discouragement.

The staff member receiving the report writes it down the same shift, and notifies [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] immediately. The Administrator or designee meets with the resident, searches the likely areas with the resident's cooperation, and interviews staff on duty.

If theft, exploitation or abuse is suspected, the Administrator follows SAF-01 for mandated reporting and SAF-02 and REC-02 for incident reports and notices to the state. The Administrator also notifies the resident's representative and, where a crime is suspected, offers to help the resident contact local law enforcement.

The Administrator completes the investigation promptly, tells the resident and representative the outcome in writing, and takes corrective action, which may include staff discipline, process changes, or reimbursement where the facility's own error or staff caused the loss.
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (STF-03). The Administrator reviews all theft and loss reports quarterly for patterns as part of internal quality review (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Decides whether the facility will hold resident cash, funds the surety bond, and ensures no facility funds are mixed with resident funds.
Files LIC 400 and LIC 402 if applicable, oversees accounts and reconciliations, investigates theft and loss reports, and makes required reports.
Handles resident funds only as authorized, issues receipts, keeps ledgers, and reports discrepancies immediately.
Safeguard resident property, never take or borrow resident money or property, and report any theft or loss immediately.

documentation: Written decision on holding resident cash
LIC 400 affidavit and LIC 402 surety bond (if applicable)
Resident authorization forms, receipts and individual ledgers
Monthly account reconciliations signed by the Administrator
Resident property and valuables inventories
Theft and loss reports, investigation notes and outcome letters
Written theft and loss policy retained as LIC 281 attachment B14

policies.title: Advance Directives and Resuscitative Measures
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all direct care staff, residents and their representatives
federal: Federal Patient Self-Determination Act principles are followed as good practice. The Act's provider requirements do not apply to RCFEs as a provider type.
policies.purpose: To respect each resident's right to accept or refuse medical care and to make known his or her wishes about resuscitation, while ensuring staff respond correctly and immediately in a medical emergency.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] respects the right of every resident to receive or reject medical care (22 CCR §87468.1). The facility will follow California's regulatory requirements for advance directives and requests regarding resuscitative measures. Staff will call 9-1-1 immediately when a resident faces an imminent threat to health (22 CCR §87465), except where a valid advance directive or resuscitative-measures request is on file and the regulation allows that request to be honored. Staff do not make medical judgments about whether a directive applies. When there is doubt about the document or its validity, staff call 9-1-1. Any use of an automated external defibrillator (AED) is reported to the licensing agency in writing within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). The facility does not require or discourage an advance directive as a condition of admission or continued stay.

definitions.definition: A written document, such as an advance health care directive or durable power of attorney for health care, stating a person's health care wishes or naming an agent to decide for them.
A resident's request, in the form recognized by California law and regulation, that resuscitation not be attempted, such as a Prehospital Do Not Resuscitate form or a POLST.
A sudden condition that endangers a resident's life or health and calls for emergency medical response.
Automated external defibrillator.

procedures: At the pre-admission appraisal and admission, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee asks each applicant, in a neutral way, whether he or she has an advance directive or a request regarding resuscitative measures, and records the answer in the resident's record.

If one exists, staff ask for a copy and place it in a clearly identified location in the resident's record, agreed on with the resident, where staff can reach it immediately in an emergency. The Administrator confirms the document is signed and dated as required.

Staff do not give legal or medical advice about advance directives. Residents who want help creating or changing a directive are referred to their physician, an attorney, their representative or the local Long-Term Care Ombudsman (1-800-231-4024).
The facility accepts a resident's or representative's updated or revoked directive at any time. Staff replace the document in the record the same day and tell all shifts at the next shift change.
New and updated directives and resuscitative-measures requests are noted in the individual service plan (ADM-03), and the representative and physician are told the facility has the document on file.

In any emergency, the first staff member on the scene checks the resident's condition and calls 9-1-1 immediately if there is an imminent threat to health, unless a valid directive or request on file lets staff withhold resuscitation as permitted by regulation.

If a valid resuscitative-measures request is on file, staff follow it as the regulation allows, call 9-1-1 as needed for other emergency care, and give the document to emergency responders on request. If staff are uncertain about the document, they call 9-1-1 and begin emergency response.
Staff trained in CPR and first aid (STF-03) give emergency care until responders arrive, unless a valid request on file says otherwise. An AED is used only by trained staff if the facility has one.

A staff member stays with the resident until emergency responders arrive and gives them the face sheet, medication list, and any directive or request on file. Another staff member notifies the representative and the Administrator.
Within the same shift, staff document in the resident's record what happened, the time 9-1-1 was called, and the resident's condition and response. The Administrator is told at once.
If an AED was used, the Administrator submits a written report to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident within 7 days (SAF-02, REC-02).
If a resident dies, staff follow HCS-10, including honoring any directive on file and making required reports.
The Administrator reviews all resident records each year, and whenever there is a change of condition (HCS-05), to confirm each directive is current and accessible.
All direct care staff are trained at orientation and annually on where directives are stored, when to call 9-1-1, and how to respond when a resuscitative-measures request is on file.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures directives are asked about, filed, accessible and current, trains staff, and files the 7-day report after any AED use.
Know where directives are kept, call 9-1-1 for imminent threats to health, provide emergency care consistent with training, and document the event.
Provide a current copy of any directive and tell the facility of any change.
Completes medical orders and forms relating to resuscitative measures for the resident.

documentation: Resident record entry of directive status at admission
Copy of advance directive or resuscitative-measures request, with date received
Individual service plan notation
Emergency response notes and incident reports
AED use report to licensing and the person responsible (7 days)
Staff training records

policies.title: Privacy, Confidentiality and HIPAA
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, contractors, residents and representatives of [AGENCY NAME]
federal: 45 CFR 164.530 (applies only if [AGENCY NAME] is a HIPAA covered entity, for example by billing Medi-Cal or another payer electronically)
policies.purpose: To protect resident privacy and the confidentiality of personal and health information, to honor the rights to private telephone calls and unopened mail, and to set clear rules about who may see resident records.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] keeps resident information confidential and shares it only as the resident or representative authorizes, or as law and licensing regulations permit or require. Residents have the right to make and receive confidential phone calls and to receive unopened mail (22 CCR §87468.1). Resident representatives are informed regularly of care activities as appropriate (22 CCR §87468.1). The admission agreement tells residents that the Department may examine resident records (22 CCR §87507). The Administrator determines in writing whether the facility is a HIPAA covered entity. If it is, the facility follows 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164, including the Notice of Privacy Practices, minimum necessary use, and a designated privacy official. If it is not, the facility still applies the confidentiality practices below as a matter of policy.

definitions.definition: Any information about a resident's identity, health, care, finances, behavior or family that is held in any form.
A health care provider that transmits health information electronically in connection with standard transactions, such as billing a health plan, and so is subject to 45 CFR Parts 160 and 164.
A person legally empowered to act for the resident, or a person the resident has chosen in writing to receive information.

procedures: Within 30 days of licensure, and again at each annual policy review, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] decides and records whether the facility is a HIPAA covered entity, after checking how it bills and communicates electronically with any payer.

If the facility is a covered entity, the Administrator names a privacy official, adopts a Notice of Privacy Practices, gives it to residents at admission and obtains a signed acknowledgment, and follows 45 CFR 164.530 administrative requirements.

Resident records are kept in a locked cabinet or in a password-protected system, and are accessible only to staff who need them to perform their duties. Records are never left open or unattended in common areas.
Staff discuss resident information only with those who need it for care, and never in hallways, dining rooms or other places where visitors or other residents can hear.

Staff may release information to others only with the resident's (or representative's) written, dated authorization specifying what is shared, with whom and for how long. Exceptions are emergencies, required reports (SAF-01, REC-02) and access by regulators and the ombudsman under RR-03.
Residents have access to their own records on request, and staff help them review them. The Administrator responds to requests for copies promptly and records each request.

The facility gives residents access to a telephone where calls can be made and received in private, for example a cordless phone in a private room or quiet area. Staff do not listen to or screen calls.
Staff deliver mail unopened. Staff may read or open a resident's mail only at the resident's request.

The Administrator or designee keeps residents' representatives informed of care activities, health changes and incidents promptly and appropriately, consistent with what the resident has authorized. Notifications are recorded in the resident's record.

Staff obtain written consent before photographing, filming or publishing a resident's image or information, including on social media or in marketing materials. Staff may not post any resident information or photos on personal social media.
Staff must use a private space for personal care, examinations, and sensitive conversations. Staff knock and wait for permission before entering a resident's room whenever possible.
Residents' names, room numbers and health conditions are not posted in public areas except where needed for safety, and then only the minimum necessary.
When records are retired, they are kept and destroyed as required by REC-01, with shredding of paper records and secure erasure of electronic records.

Staff must report any suspected breach of confidentiality to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator investigates, mitigates harm, notifies the resident or representative, and, if the facility is a covered entity, carries out any breach notification steps required by 45 CFR Part 164.
All staff sign a confidentiality statement at hire and are retrained at orientation and annually (STF-03). Violations result in corrective action up to termination.

responsibilities.duty: Decides HIPAA status, serves as or appoints the privacy official, controls record access, investigates breaches and trains staff.
Protect resident information, use it only as needed for their work, and report breaches immediately.
Provide written authorization for disclosure to others, and tell the facility of changes in who may receive information.

documentation: Written HIPAA covered-entity determination
Notice of Privacy Practices and signed acknowledgments (if covered)
Signed releases and authorizations
Staff confidentiality statements and training records
Records access request log
Breach and privacy incident reports and follow-up

policies.title: Nondiscrimination, SOGI/HIV Protections and Language Access
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, residents, applicants and representatives of [AGENCY NAME]
federal: Title VI of the Civil Rights Act (42 USC 2000d), if the facility receives federal financial assistance
policies.purpose: To ensure that every applicant and resident is treated with dignity and without discrimination, including the protections for sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression and HIV status, and that residents with disabilities or limited English can understand and take part in their care and agreements.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not deny admission to, transfer, discharge, or evict any person based on actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (22 CCR §87468.1). The same protections cover room sharing, room and restroom assignment (transgender residents are assigned by gender identity), use of the preferred name and pronouns, clothing and cosmetics, association with others, and consensual relations. A facility-wide restriction or ban on sexual relations is permitted only if applied uniformly to all residents and given in writing to residents, representatives and prospective residents before they sign the admission agreement. The Department cannot waive these protections. The facility also complies with the ADA and, if it receives federal financial assistance, with Title VI. Staff will give effective communication aids and language assistance so that every resident can understand information, including the admission agreement, and use LIC 9158 when the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability.

definitions.definition: Sexual orientation, gender identity and gender expression.
A person's internal sense of being male, female, both, neither or another gender.
A limited ability to speak, read, write or understand English, so that a person needs language help to communicate effectively.
The Department's form used when the pre-admission appraisal shows the resident has a hearing or other disability, to document how communication needs will be met.

procedures: [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] makes sure that admission, retention, transfer and eviction decisions rest only on the criteria in the admission policies (ADM-01) and the legal grounds for eviction (ADM-06), never on SOGI, HIV status or other protected characteristics.
At the pre-admission appraisal, staff ask applicants how they would like to be addressed and record the preferred name, pronouns and any communication or language needs in the resident's record.
Staff use the resident's preferred name and pronouns at all times in conversation, signage, records, name tags and menus, and ensure all shifts are informed.

Rooms and restrooms are assigned according to the resident's gender identity. Room-sharing decisions take the resident's own preferences into account, and a resident cannot be refused a roommate or room because of SOGI or HIV status.
Residents may dress and use cosmetics consistent with their gender identity and expression, and may associate with other residents, family and friends of their choice, including in private visits.
Staff do not disclose a resident's HIV status, sexual orientation or gender identity without the resident's written consent, except as the law requires (RR-07).

If [AGENCY NAME] chooses a facility-wide restriction on sexual relations, the Administrator writes the rule, applies it equally to all residents regardless of orientation or gender identity, and gives it in writing to residents, representatives and prospective residents before the admission agreement is signed. Consensual relations among residents otherwise are respected.
Staff use standard infection-control precautions for all residents (SAF-07) and never treat HIV status as a reason for different treatment or separate dining, activities or housing.

At the pre-admission appraisal, staff identify any hearing impairment, vision loss, cognitive limitation, or limited English. If the appraisal shows a hearing or other disability, the Administrator completes LIC 9158 and records how communication will be provided.

The facility provides, at no cost to the resident, qualified interpreters, translated documents, large print, or other aids as needed. Family members are not relied on for interpretation unless the resident requests it. Staff write down the aid provided.

The Administrator reviews the admission agreement with each applicant in a way the applicant can understand, in plain language and in the applicant's language when possible, and allows time and the presence of a representative.

The Administrator makes reasonable modifications to policies and the physical environment for residents with disabilities, consistent with the ADA, unless doing so would fundamentally change the service or create an undue burden.

Residents who believe they were treated unfairly may file a grievance under RR-02 without retaliation. They may also contact the licensing agency at [LOCAL CCL REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE] or the Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-800-231-4024. Staff post this information.

Any staff member who sees or hears of discriminatory treatment or harassment of a resident reports it to the Administrator the same day. The Administrator investigates promptly and takes corrective action, up to termination of employment.
All staff are trained on this policy at orientation and annually (STF-03), including respectful, culturally competent care for LGBTQ+ residents and residents living with HIV.

responsibilities.duty: Adopts and enforces this policy and provides resources for language and communication aids.
Ensures nondiscriminatory admission and discharge decisions, completes LIC 9158 when required, arranges language assistance, and investigates complaints.
Treat residents respectfully, use preferred names and pronouns, protect confidentiality, and report discrimination.

documentation: Pre-admission appraisal notes on preferred name, pronouns and communication needs
LIC 9158 (when required)
Records of interpreter, translation and communication aids provided
Written notice of any facility-wide sexual relations rule, with signed receipt
Grievances and investigation records
Staff training records

policies.title: Resident Council
policies.applies_to: Administrator, staff, residents and representatives of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To give residents an organized, protected way to voice opinions, make suggestions about facility policies and services, and take part in the life of the community.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] supports a Resident Council so that residents can discuss facility concerns, suggest changes to policies, and take part in planning activities, menus and other services. Participation is voluntary. Residents are free to meet without staff present, and no resident will be retaliated against for taking part, speaking up or declining to take part. The admission agreement tells residents how they can suggest policy changes. The Administrator checks the current Title 22 requirements for resident councils at each annual policy review (GOV-04) and updates this policy to match.

definitions.definition: A group of residents who meet to discuss and make suggestions about the facility's services, rules and community life.
A resident chosen by the council to organize meetings and speak for the group.

procedures: At admission, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee explains the Resident Council to each resident and representative, including how the resident may take part and how to suggest policy changes. The admission agreement (RR-04) includes this information.
Within 60 days after opening, the Administrator invites all residents to an organizational meeting to decide whether to form a council, how often to meet, and how officers will be chosen.

The council sets its own meeting schedule with input from residents. The Administrator posts the schedule, time and place at least [NUMBER] days before each meeting in a place visible to residents, and individually invites residents who cannot read the postings.

The facility provides an accessible space and reasonable help with notices, large print and hearing assistance so residents with disabilities can take part. Family members and representatives may attend if the residents wish.
Residents choose whether staff attend. The council may meet privately, and the Administrator attends only on invitation, or to answer questions that the council has asked to have addressed.

A resident officer or a designated staff member serving as facilitator (when the residents ask for one) takes written minutes of each meeting, listing the concerns and suggestions raised, without recording personal remarks about individual residents.

The Administrator receives the council's written concerns and suggestions within 3 business days after each meeting, and gives a written or verbal response to the council within 14 days, explaining what action will be taken or why a suggestion cannot be adopted.
Concerns that involve a complaint or an individual resident's rights are handled under the grievance process (RR-02), with the resident's consent if the concern identifies a resident.
Staff encourage participation and never discourage, retaliate against, or treat residents differently for attending, speaking or declining to attend.
Suggestions about facility policy are tracked on a log, and results are brought to the next council meeting. Actions adopted are reflected in the policy manual under GOV-04.
The Administrator reports the number and kind of council suggestions and responses at quarterly internal quality review (GOV-05).
If residents choose not to form a council, the Administrator offers again at least annually, and uses other methods such as comment forms and individual conversations to hear residents' views.

responsibilities.duty: Offers the council, provides space and support, responds in writing to concerns, and prevents retaliation.
Lead meetings, gather residents' concerns and take them to the Administrator.
Help with notices, accessibility needs and meeting logistics when asked by residents.

documentation: Notice of meetings
Minutes of Resident Council meetings
Log of suggestions and the Administrator's responses
Records of annual offer to form a council, if none exists

policies.title: Pre-Admission Appraisal, Suitability Evaluation and Admission Criteria
policies.applies_to: Administrator, admissions staff, applicants and their representatives
policies.purpose: To make sure every person admitted to [AGENCY NAME] has been appraised before admission, has consented, and is suitable for the services the facility is licensed and staffed to provide, and to give applicants the information they need before they sign.
policies.policy: No person will be admitted to [AGENCY NAME] until a pre-admission appraisal has been completed. The appraisal is an interview and a functional, mental and social evaluation, done with the applicant's consent, and it ends in a written determination of suitability against the facility's admission criteria (22 CCR §87457). The facility will not admit a person who needs health services for, or has, a prohibited health condition under 22 CCR §87615, including stage 3 or 4 pressure injuries, gastrostomy tubes, naso-gastric tubes, staph or other serious infection, total dependence on others for all activities of daily living, and tracheostomies, nor any other condition on or similar to that list. The admission criteria are part of the facility's plan of operation (22 CCR §87208). Admission decisions will not be based on actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (22 CCR §87468.1; RR-08). Applicants may visit before residence with their representatives.

definitions.definition: The written evaluation of an applicant's functional capabilities, mental condition, social background and needs, completed with the applicant's consent before admission.
The Administrator's written conclusion, based on the appraisal, that the facility can meet the applicant's needs within its license, staffing and admission criteria.
A condition that bars admission or retention under 22 CCR §87615.
The written standards in the plan of operation that determine who the facility can accept.

procedures: The Administrator writes the facility's admission criteria and includes them in the plan of operation (GOV-04). The criteria state the services the facility provides, the staffing available, and the prohibited health conditions (ADM-04, ADM-05).

When an inquiry is received, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME] or designee explains the facility's services, rates, admission criteria and the way the process works, and offers a tour. Applicants and their representatives may visit before moving in and may bring their representative.

The Administrator or a designee trained in appraisal conducts the interview in person, before admission, with the applicant and, if the applicant wishes, a representative. The applicant gives written consent to the appraisal before it starts.

The appraisal records the applicant's physical and functional abilities (including mobility and all activities of daily living), mental and cognitive condition, behavior, social history, medication needs, communication, vision and hearing, preferences, and any support needs.

The Administrator obtains the applicant's medical information from the physician as needed, and reviews the applicant's current conditions and medication list against 22 CCR §87615 and the facility's criteria.

The Administrator checks whether the applicant has any prohibited health condition, or needs services the facility cannot lawfully or practically provide. If so, the facility does not admit the person, tells the applicant and representative in writing why, and helps them find more suitable options.

If the appraisal shows that the applicant is deaf, hearing-impaired or has another disability affecting communication, the Administrator completes LIC 9158 and records how the facility will meet those needs (RR-08).

The Administrator reviews staffing, including night coverage, and the physical plant to confirm the facility can meet the applicant's needs, including any dementia care needs (HCS-06) and any ambulation or evacuation needs (SAF-06).

The Administrator signs and dates a written suitability determination stating whether the person is accepted, accepted with conditions, or declined, and the reasons. The determination is made before admission and filed in the resident's record.

Before the applicant pays anything, staff provide the proposed admission agreement. They explain any preadmission fee, what it covers, and the terms for its refund, and give the applicant time to review the agreement with a representative (RR-04).

Before the applicant signs, the Administrator tells the applicant in writing about any foreclosure, bankruptcy, unlawful detainer, rent default notice or utility shut-off notice affecting the facility in the circumstances covered by 22 CCR §87211 (REC-02).

Admission is not completed until the applicant or representative has signed the admission agreement within the time allowed under RR-04, and the appraisal findings are used to begin the individual service plan (ADM-03).
The Administrator keeps the appraisal and the suitability determination in the resident's file as part of the resident record (REC-01) and compares them with the first reassessment (ADM-02).

If the applicant is declined, the Administrator keeps a record of the inquiry and the reason, without using any protected characteristic, and tells the applicant and representative verbally and in writing.
The Administrator reviews admission decisions each quarter for consistency with the criteria and for any pattern of discrimination, as part of internal review (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Conducts or oversees the appraisal, makes the suitability determination, completes LIC 9158 when needed, and ensures no prohibited conditions are admitted.
Provide information, tours and documents to applicants, and help schedule the appraisal.
Give accurate information about the applicant's health, abilities and needs, and consent to the appraisal.
Approves the admission criteria and makes sure staffing and the physical plant match them.

documentation: Written consent to pre-admission appraisal
Completed pre-admission appraisal
Signed and dated suitability determination
LIC 9158 (when required)
Preadmission fee disclosure and receipts
Written notice to applicants of facility financial events before signing
Admission criteria in the plan of operation
Records of declined applicants and reasons

policies.title: Resident Assessment and Reassessment
policies.applies_to: All residents of [AGENCY NAME], an RCFE licensed by CDSS Community Care Licensing; administrator, designated substitute, and direct care staff
policies.purpose: To make sure every resident receives a documented pre-admission appraisal and is reassessed over time, so that the facility knows each resident's needs, admits only residents it can serve, and notices changes in condition early.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] completes a pre-admission interview and a functional, mental and social evaluation of every prospective resident, with the resident's consent, and decides on suitability against its admission criteria before admission (22 CCR §87457). The appraisal covers the medical, functional, mental and social areas that Title 22 requires. Each resident is reappraised on the schedule Title 22 requires and whenever the resident's condition changes. Staff are competent and sufficient in number to observe residents and recognize early signs of illness or decline (22 CCR §87411). The administrator confirms the current Title 22 reappraisal timelines and records them in the plan of operation. Whether a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision is decided through the appraisal, reappraisal or direct observation.

definitions.definition: The documented interview and evaluation of a prospective or current resident's medical, functional, mental and social status, used to decide suitability and the care the resident needs.
A repeat of the appraisal for a current resident, done on the required schedule and after a change in condition.
A new or worsening physical, cognitive, behavioral or functional status, including new illness, injury, fall, hospitalization or decline in ability to perform activities of daily living.
The administrator's written decision on whether the resident meets admission criteria and the facility can meet the resident's needs.

procedures: Before admission, the administrator or a trained designee schedules the pre-admission interview with the prospective resident and, where appropriate, the representative or family. The interview is in person where possible.

Before the appraisal begins, staff obtain the resident's (or legal representative's) consent to the appraisal and to the collection of health information, and document the consent in the appraisal record.

The administrator or designee completes the functional evaluation: ability to perform activities of daily living, mobility and ambulatory status, continence, communication, hearing and vision, and need for assistance or devices.
The administrator or designee completes the mental-condition evaluation: memory, orientation, judgment, mood and behavior, and any history of wandering, aggression or other behavioral expression.
The administrator or designee completes the social evaluation: family and support system, interests, history, preferences, and the resident's own goals for living at the facility.

The administrator obtains the medical assessment and current medication list from the resident's physician or other source Title 22 allows. Staff do not accept an assessment that is missing, unsigned or out of date.

The administrator compares the findings with the facility's admission criteria and with the prohibited and restricted health conditions in ADM-04 and ADM-05. The administrator documents the suitability determination, with reasons, before any admission is accepted.
If the appraisal shows the resident has a hearing or other disability that requires the additional form, staff complete LIC 9158 as required by the admission agreement rules (see RR-04).

If the prospective resident has dementia, the administrator uses the appraisal to decide whether awake night staff are needed and records the decision. The administrator sets staffing accordingly (see STF-01 and HCS-06).
Within the time Title 22 requires, the administrator or designee uses the appraisal to develop the individualized service plan (see ADM-03). Both documents are kept in the resident record.

The administrator or designee reappraises each resident on the Title 22 schedule recorded in the plan of operation, and promptly after any hospitalization, fall with injury, significant behavior change or other change in condition.

Direct care staff observe residents at each shift and during care. They report to the administrator or designee the same shift any early sign of illness, injury, pain, decreased intake, new confusion or behavior change.

On receiving a staff report, the administrator or designee reviews the resident, decides if a reappraisal, physician contact or emergency response is needed (see HCS-05, HCS-03), and documents the observation and action.

If a reappraisal shows the resident's needs exceed what the facility can legally or safely provide, or a prohibited condition has developed, the administrator follows ADM-04 and, where needed, ADM-06.
The administrator shares reappraisal results and any service plan changes with the resident and representative, and documents the communication.
The administrator reviews a sample of appraisals and reappraisals under GOV-05 to confirm they are complete, signed, dated and timely.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures appraisals and reappraisals are completed on time, makes the suitability determination, confirms current Title 22 timelines, and acts on changes in condition.
Performs appraisal tasks delegated by the administrator and covers reappraisal duties in the administrator's absence.
Observe residents each shift, recognize early signs of illness or decline, and report them the same shift.
Give consent, provide accurate information, and take part in the evaluation.

documentation: Signed consent to appraisal
Pre-admission appraisal (functional, mental, social) and medical assessment
Written suitability determination
Reappraisal records with dates and reason
LIC 9158, when required
Staff observation and change-in-condition notes
Record of night-supervision determination for residents with dementia

policies.title: Individualized Service Plan
policies.applies_to: All residents; administrator, designee, direct care staff, and any outside provider serving a resident
federal: 42 CFR 441.301(c) (person-centered planning for Assisted Living Waiver residents)
policies.purpose: To ensure each resident has a written plan of the services and supports they need and want, developed with the resident, followed by staff, and updated as needs change.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] develops an individualized service plan for each resident from the appraisal. The plan lists the basic services the facility provides, any additional services the resident has chosen and pays for, and how services from third parties (such as home health, hospice or private caregivers) fit with the facility's services. The resident takes part in decisions about their care. The resident's representative is regularly informed of ongoing evaluations. The admission agreement explains how third-party services relate to the service plan (22 CCR §87507). If the resident is enrolled in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver, the plan also reflects person-centered planning as required by 42 CFR 441.301(c) (see GOV-08).

definitions.definition: The resident's written plan, based on the appraisal, describing needs, services, who provides them, and the resident's preferences and goals.
The services every resident receives as defined in Title 22 and listed in the admission agreement.
Services delivered by a provider outside the facility, such as a home health agency, hospice, or private-duty caregiver.
A planning process led by the resident that reflects the resident's strengths, preferences and goals, as required for Assisted Living Waiver participants.

procedures: Within the time Title 22 requires after the appraisal is complete, the administrator or designee drafts the service plan from the appraisal findings and the resident's stated needs and preferences.

The administrator or designee meets with the resident, and with the representative if the resident wishes, to review the draft. The resident's choices on schedule, routine, food, activities and care preferences are written into the plan.
The plan states the basic services the resident will receive and any additional services selected, consistent with the services and rates in the signed admission agreement (see RR-04).

The plan states how any third-party provider's services relate to the facility's services. It names the provider, the tasks the provider performs, and the contact for coordination (see HCS-04 and HCS-09).
The plan identifies resident-specific risks such as falls, skin breakdown, wandering, or medication assistance needs, and the staff actions to address them (see HCS-07, HCS-08, SAF-03, HCS-02).
The resident (or representative) signs and dates the plan, or the file records the reason for no signature. The resident receives a copy on request.
The administrator places the plan in the resident record and makes it available to caregivers on every shift, without exposing it to unauthorized persons (see RR-07).
Direct care staff review the plan before delivering care to a new resident and after any update. The administrator documents that this review took place.
The administrator or designee updates the plan after each reappraisal, after a change in condition, after a hospitalization, and when the resident or representative requests a change (see ADM-02).
The administrator or designee informs the representative of ongoing evaluations and plan changes in a regular, documented way, with the date, method and person contacted.
If the resident disagrees with part of the plan, the administrator records the disagreement, tries to resolve it with the resident, and treats unresolved concerns under RR-02.
If the resident is enrolled in the Assisted Living Waiver, the administrator coordinates the plan with the waiver care coordinator, records the resident's own goals and choices, and follows GOV-08.
The administrator audits a sample of service plans under GOV-05 for completeness, resident participation, and match with care actually delivered.

responsibilities.duty: Ensures each resident has a current, signed plan, resident participation is documented, and third-party services are coordinated.
Drafts and updates plans under the administrator's direction.
Read and follow the plan, and report needed changes.
Take part in planning, state preferences, and review changes.

documentation: Individualized service plan with dates and signatures
Notes of resident and representative participation
Record of representative notifications of evaluations
Third-party provider coordination notes
Staff acknowledgment of plan review
Waiver person-centered plan, if applicable

policies.title: Retention Limits and Prohibited Health Conditions
policies.applies_to: Administrator, designee, direct care staff, and all prospective and current residents
policies.purpose: To prevent admission or retention of any resident who has a condition that Title 22 prohibits in an RCFE, and to make sure changes in condition are identified and acted on without delay.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not admit or retain a resident who needs health services for, or has, any of these conditions: stage 3 or stage 4 pressure injuries; gastrostomy tubes; naso-gastric tubes; staph or other serious infection; total dependence on others for all activities of daily living; or tracheostomies (22 CCR §87615). The list is not exhaustive, so the administrator reviews any other serious condition against Title 22 before admission or continued stay. Exceptions or Department review are available only as Title 22 provides, and only the administrator may request them. The facility also does not accept or keep a nonambulatory or bedridden resident without a separate fire clearance (22 CCR §87202; see ADM-05). If the Department orders a resident relocated because of a health condition, the facility complies and informs the resident of the right to request review.

definitions.definition: A condition listed in 22 CCR §87615 (and any other condition Title 22 treats the same way) that bars admission or retention of the resident in an RCFE.
A resident who relies on others for all activities of daily living.
A Department order that a resident be moved because the resident has a condition the facility may not retain.
Continuing to house a resident after admission.

procedures: During the pre-admission appraisal, the administrator screens the prospective resident's medical assessment, medication list, skin status, feeding method, airway status and ADL needs against each listed prohibited condition, and records the result.
If any prohibited condition is present or needed, the administrator does not admit the resident and gives the person and family information on alternative placement options.

The administrator also reviews the appraisal for any serious condition not named in the list and checks Title 22 and, when necessary, calls the CDSS Adult and Senior Care Program regional office at (916) 657-2592 for guidance before deciding. The call is documented.
At each reappraisal, and whenever a change in condition occurs, the administrator repeats the screening for prohibited conditions and documents it (see ADM-02).

Direct care staff check residents' skin during bathing and dressing, and report any open area, new wound, new feeding tube, breathing device, signs of serious infection, or sudden loss of independence to the administrator the same shift (see HCS-08).
On any such report, the administrator or designee assesses the resident, contacts the physician (see HCS-05), and determines whether the resident has developed a prohibited condition.

If a prohibited condition develops, the administrator does not delay action. The administrator tells the resident and representative, arranges the needed assessment or hospital evaluation, and starts the discharge planning process in ADM-06.

The administrator requests a Department exception or review only when Title 22 permits it, in writing, with the supporting physician information. The administrator keeps the request, the Department's response and the resident's plan.

If the Department issues a health condition relocation order, the administrator complies within the period stated, helps the resident find placement, and gives the resident written notice of the right to request review.
The administrator never uses staff, family or third-party providers to deliver services for a prohibited condition inside the facility as a way of avoiding relocation.
The administrator reports changes in resident status to the state where required (see REC-02, SAF-02).
The administrator reviews all retention decisions quarterly under GOV-05 and records trends.

responsibilities.duty: Screens for prohibited conditions at admission and reappraisal, decides on retention, requests exceptions only as permitted, and carries out relocation.
Assists with screening and documents findings.
Observe and report conditions that may be prohibited.
The Department may issue relocation orders and review decisions under Title 22.

documentation: Prohibited-condition screening at pre-admission and each reappraisal
Staff reports of changes in condition
Physician communications
Department exception or review requests and responses
Relocation orders and notices
Alternative placement assistance record

policies.title: Allowable and Restricted Health Conditions, Bedridden and Nonambulatory Residents (CA-specific addition)
policies.applies_to: Administrator, designee, direct care staff, and any resident with a restricted health condition, bedridden status or nonambulatory status
policies.purpose: To set conditions under which the facility may serve residents with certain restricted health conditions, or who are bedridden or nonambulatory, so that care is lawful, safe and supported by the right fire clearance, training and professional services.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] accepts or keeps a resident with a restricted health condition only if Title 22 allows that condition in an RCFE, the facility can meet the resident's needs, and all conditions of the regulation are met. Title 22 treats the following as restricted or allowable conditions, each with its own rules: oxygen, intermittent positive pressure breathing, colostomy or ileostomy, enemas or suppositories, indwelling catheters, managed incontinence, contractures, diabetes, injections, and healing wounds. A resident who is nonambulatory or bedridden may be accepted or kept only if the facility holds a separate fire clearance for nonambulatory or bedridden residents (22 CCR §87202) and meets Title 22's rules on bedridden care and ambulatory status. A home health agency or licensed professional provides the services staff may not lawfully perform (see HCS-04). Direct care staff who assist with these residents complete the required training, including 4 hours on postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice before working alone (HSC §1569.625).

definitions.definition: A condition that Title 22 allows in an RCFE only under specific rules, which may include physician orders, a licensed professional or home health agency, staff training, and written resident agreement.
A resident who is confined to bed as defined and limited by Title 22.
A resident who cannot move from place to place or leave the building in an emergency without help from another person.

definitions.term: Fire clearance for nonambulatory or bedridden residents
definitions.definition: A separate fire authority clearance that must be in place before the facility accepts or keeps such residents (22 CCR §87202).

procedures: At pre-admission, and at each reappraisal, the administrator identifies whether the resident has a restricted health condition or is bedridden or nonambulatory, and documents it (see ADM-02).

Before accepting or keeping a resident with a restricted condition, the administrator reads the specific Title 22 rule for that condition and records in the file how the facility will meet each requirement.
The administrator obtains and files the physician's written orders and instructions for the condition, including any limits on what staff may do.

If the resident has a nonambulatory or bedridden status, the administrator checks that the facility's fire clearance covers such residents before acceptance. If it does not, the facility does not accept or keep the resident until the fire authority approves it (see GOV-03, SAF-06).

The administrator confirms that the facility's physical plant, exits and evacuation plan can safely evacuate the resident, and records the evacuation method in the resident's file (see SAF-05, SAF-06).

The administrator arranges a home health agency, licensed nurse or other licensed professional for any task Title 22 does not allow unlicensed staff to perform, and records the agreement and contact (see HCS-04, HCS-09).
Direct care staff do not give injections, perform sterile procedures, or carry out any task outside what Title 22 allows, unless the law specifically authorizes it for that condition.

The administrator confirms that every staff member assigned to the resident has completed the training required before working alone, including the 4 hours on postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice, and documents it in the personnel record (see STF-03, STF-05).
Where the care of the resident requires postural supports or restraints, staff follow SAF-04 and obtain the physician order Title 22 requires.

The administrator gets the resident's agreement, where Title 22 requires it, to the restricted-condition care arrangement, and adds the care instructions to the individualized service plan (see ADM-03).

Staff monitor the resident's condition each shift and report changes to the administrator or the physician (see HCS-05). The administrator re-evaluates the resident's eligibility to stay after any report.
If the condition becomes prohibited, or the facility can no longer meet requirements, the administrator follows ADM-04 and ADM-06.
The administrator reviews the list of residents with restricted conditions, their fire clearance status and staff training monthly, and records it under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Decides on acceptance and retention, confirms the fire clearance, arranges licensed professionals, and ensures training and documentation.
Supports monitoring and records observations.
Complete required training, follow physician instructions and the service plan, and stay within the tasks Title 22 allows.
Perform nursing or medical tasks that staff may not perform.

documentation: Fire clearance covering nonambulatory or bedridden residents
Physician orders for restricted conditions
Home health or professional services agreements
Resident agreement to the restricted-condition arrangement
Evacuation method record
Staff training records, including the 4-hour postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice course
Monthly review of restricted condition residents

policies.title: Eviction, Discharge, Transfer and Relocation Notice
policies.applies_to: Administrator, designee, residents and representatives, and any discharge, transfer, eviction or closure
policies.purpose: To ensure that any eviction, discharge or transfer is based on lawful grounds, follows the required notice and complaint rights, protects the resident from discrimination, and returns refunds that are owed.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] evicts, transfers or discharges a resident only on grounds that state law or regulation provides. The grounds in the admission agreement are worded exactly as stated in those authorities and are not modified, except for general house policies the regulations allow. The facility never evicts, transfers or discharges a resident because of the resident's actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status (22 CCR §87468.1(b)). The admission agreement explains the resident's notice rights, the process for filing a complaint with the Department about an eviction, the relocation assistance the facility offers, and the licensee's responsibilities if the facility closes (22 CCR §87507). If the Department orders a resident relocated, the resident is not held to the advance-notice terms, and the facility refunds what would have been owed had notice been given. Prepaid fees and preadmission fees are refunded as specified, and preadmission fee refunds on forfeiture or closure are paid within 15 days of issuing the notice.

definitions.definition: A facility-initiated termination of residency on a ground the law allows.
A move of a resident out of the facility, whether to another residence, a hospital or another care setting.
A move required by a Department order or by closure of the facility, with the resident's rights to notice, help and refund.
The resident's right to written notice, the reasons, the time period and the right to complain, as required by state law.

procedures: Before beginning any eviction, discharge or transfer, the administrator confirms that the ground is one stated in state law or regulation and matches the exact wording in the resident's admission agreement. If it does not, the facility does not proceed.

The administrator checks that the reason is not connected to the resident's actual or perceived sexual orientation, gender identity, gender expression or HIV status. The administrator records this check.

The administrator meets with the resident and representative, explains the concern, and tries to resolve it where the law allows, such as by adjusting the service plan or arranging a licensed professional (see ADM-03, HCS-04). The meeting is documented.

When eviction or discharge is necessary, the administrator prepares the written notice with the reason, the applicable legal ground, the effective date, the period that state law requires, and the resident's rights.

The notice tells the resident how to file a complaint with the Department about the eviction (CDSS ASCP, (916) 657-2592, or the regional office at [ADDRESS/PHONE of regional office]) and how to contact the Long-Term Care Ombudsman at 1-800-231-4024.

The administrator delivers the notice to the resident and the representative in the manner the law requires, using the language and format the resident can understand (see RR-08). A signed receipt or proof of delivery is kept.

The administrator describes in writing the relocation assistance the facility will provide, such as help locating a new placement, arranging transport, transferring records and medications, and informing the physician.

In an emergency requiring immediate transfer for the resident's health, the administrator calls 9-1-1 or the physician as needed (see HCS-03, HCS-05), and follows state law on the notice and reporting steps that apply.
The administrator reports to the Department and the Ombudsman where state law requires (see REC-02, RR-03).

If the Department orders the resident's relocation, or a health condition relocation order is issued, the facility complies, informs the resident of the right to request review, and does not apply advance-notice terms against the resident.

The administrator calculates the refund of prepaid fees and, where applicable, the amount the resident would have owed had notice been given. The refund is paid as specified in the admission agreement and state law (see RR-04).

On closure, sale or license forfeiture, the administrator issues the required notice, follows the closure plan, and pays all prepaid and preadmission fee refunds, with preadmission fee refunds paid within 15 days of issuing the notice.
At departure, staff return the resident's money, valuables, property and medications and document the inventory with the resident or representative's signature (see RR-05, HCS-01).
The administrator closes the record in the register of residents and retains the file as required (see REC-01).
The administrator reviews each discharge or eviction under GOV-05 for lawful grounds, timeliness of notices, refund accuracy and absence of discrimination.

responsibilities.duty: Confirms lawful grounds, issues notices, offers relocation help, pays refunds and makes required reports.
Assists with transfer logistics and inventory under the administrator's direction.
Approves any closure plan and funds required refunds.
Receive notice, may file a complaint, and may request review.
