Record of legal ground and non-discrimination check
Resident meeting notes
Relocation assistance record
Refund calculation and payment record
Property and medication return inventory
Reports to Department and Ombudsman
Department relocation orders and responses

policies.title: Medication Management, Storage and Disposal
policies.applies_to: Administrator, designee, direct care staff who assist residents with medications, and all residents' prescription and nonprescription medications
policies.purpose: To make sure resident medications are stored, tracked and destroyed safely and as Title 22 requires, and that staff stay within the limits of assisting with self-administered medication.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] staff assist residents with self-administered medications only and do not give injections unless authorized by law. Assistance never includes forcing, hiding or camouflaging medication. PRN medication requires a signed, dated physician order on a prescription blank stating the symptoms, exact dose, minimum hours between doses and maximum doses in 24 hours (22 CCR §87465). Medications are centrally stored when refrigeration is needed and the resident has no private refrigerator, when the physician considers the medication hazardous for the resident to keep, or when it is a safety hazard to others. Centrally stored medications are kept locked, accessible only to responsible employees, in the original container, with no transfer between containers; only the dispensing pharmacist may alter a label. The facility keeps the central storage record for at least 1 year. Leftover prescription medications are destroyed at the facility by the administrator and one other non-resident adult, with a record kept at least 3 years. These procedures are part of the facility's plan of operation and incidental medical care plan (22 CCR §87208).

definitions.definition: Help allowed under Title 22 where the resident takes their own medication, such as reminders, opening containers or handing the container to the resident. It does not include administration by staff (see HCS-02).
Storage of a resident's medication by the facility in a locked place accessible only to responsible employees.
A medication taken as needed, only under a physician order that contains the elements Title 22 requires.
The signed record of leftover prescription medications destroyed at the facility.

procedures: The administrator designates the staff authorized to assist with medications and confirms they have the required training and authorization before any assistance (see HCS-02, STF-03). For a facility of 16 or more residents, the administrator also designates the staff with primary responsibility for first aid and medication assistance.
Each resident's medications are kept in the original pharmacy container. Staff never move medication to another container or change a label. Only the dispensing pharmacist may alter a label.

The administrator decides, at appraisal and when a change occurs, whether a resident's medication must be centrally stored. Reasons include refrigeration needed with no private refrigerator, a physician's finding that the medication is hazardous in the resident's possession, or safety risk to others. Reasons are documented.

Centrally stored medications are kept in a locked cabinet, drawer or refrigerator compartment. Only responsible employees named by the administrator hold keys or access codes. Keys are never left unattended.

When a medication is placed in central storage, staff create a record with the resident's name, prescriber, drug, strength, quantity, fill date, prescription number, pharmacy, and the custody instructions. The record is kept at least 1 year.
When the physician or the Department requests it, the facility keeps and provides a record of dosages of centrally stored medications.

Staff accept a PRN medication only with a signed, dated physician order on a prescription blank, listing the symptoms, exact dose, minimum hours between doses and maximum doses in 24 hours. Staff do not use a PRN without these elements and contact the physician for a corrected order.

Staff never force a resident to take a medication and never hide or camouflage it in food or drink. A resident's refusal is respected, documented and reported to the administrator, who notifies the physician (see HCS-05).
Staff do not give injections unless the law authorizes it and Title 22 conditions are met (see ADM-05, HCS-04).

Staff report a medication error, missing medication or suspected diversion to the administrator immediately. The administrator contacts the physician and pharmacy as needed, and documents the event (see SAF-02).
The administrator checks the central storage area and records at least monthly for expired, discontinued or unaccounted-for medication and updates the record.
When medications are discontinued, expired, or left after a resident dies or leaves, the administrator holds them in locked storage pending destruction or return in accordance with law.
For residents receiving hospice, the facility follows the hospice's medication disposal procedures (see HCS-09).

For all other leftover prescription medications, the administrator and one other non-resident adult destroy the medication at the facility. Both sign a record listing the resident, prescription number and pharmacy, drug, strength, quantity and the date. The record is kept at least 3 years.
The administrator reviews medication practices, storage and records quarterly under GOV-05 and retrains staff when problems appear.

responsibilities.duty: Designates authorized staff, decides on central storage, controls access, witnesses destruction, and keeps records.
Co-signs destruction records; the witness must be a non-resident adult.
Assist only within Title 22 limits, follow PRN order requirements, and report errors and refusals.
Write compliant orders, and label or alter labels (the pharmacist only).

documentation: Central storage record, kept at least 1 year
Medication destruction record, kept at least 3 years
PRN physician orders
Medication dosage record when requested by the physician or Department
Designation of staff responsible for medication and first aid
Medication error and refusal reports
Monthly storage check log

policies.title: Assistance with Self-Administered Medications and Staff Authorization (no administration by staff)
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, the Administrator, the Designated Substitute and any staff member who assists a resident with medications at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] staff only assist residents with self-administered medications as California law allows. Residents keep the right to refuse. Only trained and authorized staff provide assistance, and every dose and PRN decision is documented.
policies.policy: Staff of [AGENCY NAME] do not administer medications. Staff may only assist residents with medications that are usually self-administered and authorized by the resident's physician. This includes assistance for temporary minor illness and for residents with tremor or failing eyesight. Staff never give injections unless authorized by law. Staff never force, hide or camouflage a medication without the resident's consent, and never interfere with the resident's right to refuse. No staff member may assist with medications until the Administrator has confirmed the required medication assistance training is complete and documented. PRN (as-needed) medications are assisted only under a written physician order that meets the requirements below. Central storage and destruction of medications are governed by HCS-01, and this policy applies alongside it.

definitions.definition: Helping a resident take a medication the resident could take without help but for tremor, failing eyesight or a similar limitation, for example by opening containers, reading labels, or steadying or handing the medication to the resident. The resident remains the person taking the medication.
A medication taken only as needed for stated symptoms, under a written physician order.
The physician's written prescription or order form on which a PRN order must be written, signed and dated.
Hiding a medication in food or drink without the resident's knowledge or consent.
The resident's representative, family member or other person identified in the admission agreement or appraisal who is responsible for the resident's care decisions or notification.

procedures: The Administrator will maintain a current list of staff authorized to assist with self-administered medications. A staff member is added to the list only after the training and exam requirements in steps 2 and 3 are met and documented.

If [AGENCY NAME] is licensed for 15 or fewer residents, the Administrator will require each assisting staff member to complete 10 hours of initial medication assistance training. Six hours of hands-on training are completed before the staff member first assists a resident, and four hours are completed within 2 weeks. The staff member must also pass an exam.

If [AGENCY NAME] is licensed for 16 or more residents, the Administrator will require 24 hours of initial training. Sixteen hours of hands-on training are completed before the staff member first assists a resident, and eight hours are completed within 4 weeks. The staff member must also pass an exam.

The Administrator will schedule and track 8 hours of medication assistance training every year for every authorized staff member. A staff member whose annual hours lapse is removed from the authorized list until the hours are completed.
The Administrator will file the training certificate, exam result, trainer name and qualifications, and dates in the staff member's personnel record (see STF-05).

Before assisting any resident, the staff member will confirm that the resident has a current physician order and that the pharmacy label matches the order for resident name, medication, dose, route and time.

The staff member will wash hands, identify the resident, and offer the medication at the ordered time. The resident takes the medication. Staff may open containers, read the label aloud, steady the resident's hand or hand the medication to the resident, but may not place a medication in the resident's mouth or apply or inject it for the resident, and may not give any injection unless authorized by law.

If a resident refuses a medication, the staff member will respect the refusal, will not force, hide or camouflage the medication, and will not threaten or pressure the resident. The staff member will record the refusal on the medication record and tell the Administrator or Designated Substitute the same shift. The Administrator will notify the physician and the person responsible for the resident as the situation requires.

For every PRN medication, the Administrator will confirm before first assistance that the physician's order is on a prescription blank, signed and dated. The order must state the symptoms, the exact dose, the minimum hours between doses and the maximum number of doses in 24 hours, and the pharmacy label must match. If an order is incomplete, the staff member will not assist with the PRN and will ask the Administrator to obtain a corrected order.
If the resident can decide when a PRN is needed, the resident decides, and staff assist. Staff record each PRN dose with date, time, dose and the resident's response.

If the resident cannot decide when a PRN is needed but can communicate symptoms, staff may assist only if the physician's directions include a discontinuation time or circumstance and state when to recontact the physician. Staff record each dose with date, time, dose and response and recontact the physician as directed.

If the resident can neither decide nor communicate symptoms, staff must call the physician before every PRN dose, follow the physician's instruction, and document the call (date, time, person spoken to, instruction given) and the dose given.
Staff will lock medications in central storage in their original containers as required by HCS-01, and will never leave medications unattended during assistance.

Any medication error, missed dose, wrong-resident event or adverse reaction will be reported to the Administrator the same shift. The Administrator will notify the physician and person responsible for the resident, and will evaluate whether the event is reportable under SAF-02 and REC-02.

Any staff member who is asked to give an injection, administer a medication, or perform a task beyond assistance will decline, notify the Administrator, and see HCS-04 for referral to a licensed professional or home health agency.
The Administrator will review medication records at least monthly for gaps, PRN use patterns, refusals and discrepancies, and will document the review and corrective action under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Provide resources so only trained staff assist with medications and so annual training is completed.
Maintain the authorized staff list, verify training and exams, obtain compliant PRN orders, review records monthly, and investigate errors.
Carry out Administrator duties in this policy when the Administrator is absent.
Assist only within the limits of this policy, respect refusals, record each dose or refusal accurately, and report errors the same shift.
Provide compliant written orders and labels, and respond to staff calls about PRN use and changes.

documentation: Medication assistance training certificates, exam results and trainer qualifications in personnel records
Authorized staff list with dates of training and annual renewal
Medication record for each resident showing date, time, dose, staff initials and refusals
Signed and dated physician orders, including PRN orders on prescription blanks
PRN dose record with date, time, dose and response
Physician call log for residents who cannot decide or communicate PRN need
Medication error and refusal notes and Administrator monthly review notes

policies.title: Incidental Medical and Dental Care and Emergency Response
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Designated Substitute and all direct care staff at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure residents receive prompt, appropriate incidental medical and dental care and that staff respond correctly and report required events to the state.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written plan for incidental medical and dental care. The plan covers arranging or assisting with care and providing transportation, which may be limited to the nearest available facility that meets the resident's need. Staff call 9-1-1 immediately when there is an imminent threat to a resident's health. A complete first aid kit is kept in a known location, and emergency numbers, physician and dentist contacts and an ambulance number are posted or readily available. Any use of an automated external defibrillator (AED) is reported to the licensing agency in writing within 7 days. Medication assistance is limited as described in HCS-02.

definitions.definition: Routine health services that are arranged or assisted by the facility, such as appointments, transportation to care and help using aids, but not nursing care provided by staff.
A sudden condition that could cause death or serious harm without immediate emergency response, such as unresponsiveness, chest pain, severe bleeding or choking.
Automated external defibrillator, a device used to treat sudden cardiac arrest.
CDSS Community Care Licensing, Adult and Senior Care Program.

procedures: The Administrator will adopt and keep current a written incidental medical and dental care plan that covers how care is arranged, how transportation is provided (including the nearest available facility that meets the need), and who is responsible. The plan is reviewed at least annually with the plan of operation (GOV-04).

At admission and at each reappraisal, the Administrator will record each resident's physician, dentist, preferred hospital, pharmacy, insurance and the person responsible for the resident, and will keep this information readily available to staff.

The Administrator will post emergency numbers (9-1-1, poison control, local fire and police, the licensing agency, the ombudsman, [AGENCY NAME] Administrator at [PHONE] and the ambulance service) near each telephone, and will keep an ambulance service number readily available.

The Administrator will maintain a complete first aid kit in a location known to all staff. The kit contains a first aid manual, sterile dressings, bandages, scissors, tweezers and thermometers. The Administrator or designee will inspect the kit monthly and after use, restock it, and record the inspection date.

At orientation, the Administrator will train each staff member on the location of the first aid kit, the emergency numbers, and how to use residents' prosthetics, hearing aids and vision aids. Staff must keep these aids clean, in working order and available to the resident, and report loss or damage to the Administrator the same shift.

When staff find a resident with an imminent threat to health, they will call 9-1-1 immediately, begin first aid within their training, and stay with the resident. Staff must not delay 9-1-1 to reach the Administrator or family.

After calling 9-1-1, staff will notify the Administrator or Designated Substitute, then the resident's physician and the person responsible for the resident without delay. Staff will send the resident's face sheet, medication list and advance directive information with the resident (see RR-06 for resuscitative measures).

If an AED is used, staff will document the event as soon as safely possible. The Administrator will submit a written report to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident within 7 days.

For any death, serious injury as determined by the physician, or incident threatening welfare, safety or health, the Administrator will submit a written report to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days. For outbreaks, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents, the Administrator will notify the licensing agency and the local health officer by phone or fax within 24 hours. For fires and explosions, staff will call the local fire authority immediately, and the Administrator will notify the licensing agency no later than the next working day. Use SAF-02 and REC-02 for report content and filing.

For non-emergency needs, staff will help the resident schedule appointments with the physician or dentist, ensure the resident or representative is informed of the appointment, provide or arrange transportation (see DL-04), and send needed information with the resident.

After a medical or dental visit, staff will obtain orders, medication changes and follow-up instructions, give them to the Administrator the same day, and update the medication record and service plan. The Administrator will arrange reassessment if the change in condition is significant (see HCS-05 and ADM-02).
Staff will not perform treatments or procedures beyond their training or beyond what the law allows. See HCS-04 for referral to a licensed professional or home health agency.
The Administrator will review each emergency response within 3 business days to evaluate timeliness, communication and needed corrective action, and will document the review under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the written plan, posted numbers and first aid kit, train staff, make required reports, and review each emergency response.
Carry out these duties when the Administrator is absent.
Recognize emergencies, call 9-1-1 without delay, give first aid within their training, notify the Administrator, and care for residents' aids.
Provide supplies, training time and equipment, including any AED.

documentation: Written incidental medical and dental care plan
Resident contact and provider information sheet
Posted emergency numbers and ambulance number (date verified)
First aid kit inspection log
Staff training records on first aid kit, aids and emergency response
Emergency response notes and Administrator review
AED use report and written reports to licensing, with proof of submission and notice to the person responsible
Appointment, transportation and follow-up records

policies.title: Licensed Professionals, Home Health Agencies and Limits on Staff Nursing Tasks
policies.applies_to: All [AGENCY NAME] employees, volunteers, contracted staff, visiting licensed professionals, and home health or hospice agencies serving residents of the Residential Care Facility for the Elderly (RCFE)
policies.purpose: To make clear that [AGENCY NAME] is a licensed RCFE and not a nursing facility. This policy sets out which tasks facility staff may and may not perform, how skilled or specialized care is obtained from properly licensed professionals and home health agencies, and how care is coordinated so residents stay safe and the facility stays within its license.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] staff are not licensed nursing staff. Staff will not perform nursing procedures that require a licensed professional. Under 22 CCR §87411, services that require specialized skills are performed only by personnel qualified by training or experience, and personnel must be sufficient in number and competent. Under 22 CCR §87465, staff may only assist with self-administered medications and may not give injections unless authorized by law. Staff will never force, hide or camouflage medications. When a resident needs skilled nursing, therapy or other professional services, including services tied to an allowable health condition, these are delivered by an appropriately licensed professional or a licensed home health agency (or hospice agency) and not by facility caregivers. The Administrator must approve the arrangement, confirm that the care can be met within the facility's license and Plan of Operation, and make sure it is coordinated in writing with the resident's Individualized Service Plan. Federal home health agency rules apply to the agencies themselves and do not make the facility a home health provider. Night and general staffing must stay adequate while outside professionals are in the building, in line with 22 CCR §87415 and STF-01. If the facility is enrolled in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver, the additional nursing and oversight requirements in GOV-08 also apply.

definitions.definition: A person who holds a current California license or certification for the service provided, such as a registered nurse, licensed vocational nurse, physician, physical or occupational therapist, or dentist.

A separately licensed agency that sends licensed professionals to a resident's residence to provide skilled nursing, therapy or related services under a physician's order. It is not part of the facility and is not supervised by the facility.

Any procedure that requires a nursing or other health license, or that the law does not authorize unlicensed RCFE staff to perform. Examples are administering medications to residents, giving injections unless authorized by law, and assessing or staging wounds.

Helping a resident who is able to take their own medication, for example by reminding them, opening containers, or steadying a hand, without staff making the decision for the resident or administering the medication.
A staff member who has documented training, and where applicable a license or certificate, for the specialized service, with the qualification recorded in the personnel record.

procedures: The Administrator, [ADMINISTRATOR NAME], reviews this policy with every new employee during orientation and with all staff each year. Each person signs an acknowledgment that is filed in the personnel record.

Staff tasks are limited to personal care and supervision, assistance with self-administered medications under HCS-01 and HCS-02, and first aid and emergency response under HCS-03. Staff must not perform any task that requires a license or that the law does not authorize them to do.

Staff do not give injections. Before any exception is considered, the Administrator confirms with CDSS Community Care Licensing at (916) 657-2592 and with the resident's physician that the law specifically authorizes the task, and documents the answer. Until that is done, the task is arranged through a licensed professional or home health agency.
Staff never force, hide or camouflage medications. They do not decide whether a resident needs a PRN medication unless the physician's PRN order is written as required by HCS-01.

During the pre-admission appraisal and each reassessment (ADM-01 and ADM-02), the Administrator or designee identifies any need for skilled nursing, therapy, wound care, injections or other services that exceed staff scope. The need is recorded in the appraisal and the Individualized Service Plan (ADM-03).

When such a need exists, the Administrator decides whether the resident's care can be met at the facility. This includes whether the need relates to an allowable or restricted health condition under ADM-04 and ADM-05, and whether it requires a licensed professional or home health agency to provide the service on site.

If the care can be met, the resident or the resident's representative selects and arranges a licensed home health agency or other licensed professional. The Administrator helps by providing a list of options when asked, but does not direct the choice.

Before services begin, the Administrator obtains or documents the agency's name, contact person, the physician's order, the services and visit schedule, and an emergency contact number. The Administrator records this in the resident's record.

On the first visit, the Administrator or designee sees the professional's current license or agency identification, introduces the professional to the shift lead, and confirms where the professional will work. Visitor sign-in is used to record entry and exit.

Facility staff do not carry out nursing orders given by an outside professional unless the task is within staff scope. The professional or agency instructs staff in writing on observations to report, such as changes in skin, breathing or intake. Staff report these observations to the agency and the Administrator.

The shift lead and the agency nurse exchange information at each visit about changes in the resident's condition. The shift lead records the visit and any new instructions in the resident's record and informs the Administrator the same day.

If staff observe a change of condition, an unsafe practice, or a problem with agency services, the shift lead notifies the Administrator immediately. The Administrator contacts the agency's supervisor, and the resident's physician and representative as needed under HCS-05, and documents the contact.

The Administrator keeps staffing adequate while outside professionals are present. Visiting professionals are never counted as facility staff. Night supervision follows 22 CCR §87415 and STF-01: with fewer than 16 residents, a qualified person is on call on the premises overnight; with 16 to 100 residents, one employee is awake on duty and one is on call within 10 minutes. Night staff must know the emergency plan and be first-aid trained.

Staff who give personal care to residents receive the initial and annual training and the first aid training required under 22 CCR §87411 and STF-03. The Administrator checks that each staff member's qualification matches the tasks assigned, and records it in the personnel record.

If the facility is enrolled in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver, the Administrator follows GOV-08 for any licensed nursing staff on call or employed and for LVN oversight, and keeps that documentation with the waiver records.

If a resident's needs grow beyond what the facility, even with a home health agency, can safely and lawfully provide, the Administrator begins the process in ADM-06 and notifies the resident's representative, physician and, where appropriate, the Ombudsman.

The Administrator reviews each active home health or professional arrangement at least quarterly, and at each reassessment, to confirm that the service is still needed and is being delivered, and records the review in the resident's record.

Any occurrence in which a staff member performs a task beyond scope, or in which a resident is harmed during skilled care, is reported to the Administrator immediately. It is documented and, where required, reported under SAF-02 and REC-02. Corrective action and retraining are recorded in the personnel record.

responsibilities.duty: Enforces scope-of-practice limits, approves arrangements with outside professionals and agencies, verifies that staff are qualified for assigned tasks, keeps staffing adequate, and documents coordination and reviews.
Perform only tasks within staff scope, report changes in condition and any request to perform outside-scope tasks, and record agency visits and instructions.
Chooses and arranges the home health agency or professional, and provides orders and contact information.
Provides skilled services under physician orders, communicates in writing with the facility, and supervises its own personnel.
Issues orders for skilled services and PRN medications, and advises on the resident's condition as requested.

documentation: Signed staff acknowledgment of scope-of-practice limits (personnel record)
Pre-admission appraisal, reassessment and Individualized Service Plan entries identifying needs beyond staff scope
Home health or professional arrangement record: agency name, contact, physician order, services and schedule
Visitor sign-in log and verification of professional license or agency identification
Communication notes with home health agencies, and shift log entries
Quarterly review notes for each outside-service arrangement
Incident reports and corrective action for out-of-scope tasks
Training and first aid records in personnel files
If enrolled in the Assisted Living Waiver, nursing staff and oversight records per GOV-08

policies.title: Change of Condition, Physician Notification and Hospital Transfer
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Designated Substitute and all direct care staff at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To ensure staff recognize early signs of illness, respond to emergencies, notify physicians and representatives, report required events to the state, and manage hospital transfer and return safely.
policies.policy: Staff of [AGENCY NAME] observe residents daily and recognize early signs of illness or decline. They report changes to the Administrator the same shift. Staff call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to health. The Administrator ensures the physician and the person responsible for the resident are notified, a reassessment is done after a significant change, and the service plan is updated. Any death, serious injury as determined by the physician, or incident threatening welfare, safety or health is reported in writing to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days. Before a resident returns from a hospital or other facility, the Administrator evaluates whether the resident still meets admission and retention requirements.

definitions.definition: A noticeable change in a resident's physical, mental, emotional or functional status, such as new confusion, fever, loss of appetite, fall, new pain, change in mobility, or change in behavior.
A sudden condition that may result in death or serious harm without immediate emergency care.
A review of the resident's needs and abilities after a change to decide whether the resident's needs can still be met and what the service plan should say.
The resident's representative, family member or other person identified in the admission agreement or appraisal.

procedures: At orientation and annually, the Administrator will train staff to recognize early signs of illness and change, including fever, cough, dehydration, confusion, new pain, skin changes, falls, change in eating, toileting or sleeping, and withdrawal.
Staff will observe each resident at each contact and at scheduled checks, and will record notable observations in the resident's daily notes.
When staff notice a change of condition, they will report it to the Administrator or Designated Substitute before the end of the shift, or immediately if the change is acute.
If the resident shows signs of an imminent threat to health, staff will call 9-1-1 first, give first aid within their training, and then notify the Administrator.

For non-emergency changes, the Administrator or designee will call the resident's physician the same day, report observations clearly, and request instructions. The staff member will record the date and time, the person spoken to and the instructions given.

If the physician gives orders or medication changes, staff will follow HCS-02 for medication assistance. For PRN decisions for a resident who cannot decide or communicate symptoms, staff will call the physician before every dose and document the contact.

The Administrator will notify the person responsible for the resident of the change and of any physician instructions the same day, or as soon as the person can be reached. The Administrator will record the notification.

The Administrator will evaluate whether the resident requires a reassessment (ADM-02) and a service plan update (ADM-03). The Administrator will also evaluate whether the resident's needs exceed what the facility can meet or whether the condition is prohibited (ADM-04, ADM-05). If so, the Administrator will begin the process in ADM-06 and will not give notice without following its requirements.

If the resident is sent to a hospital, staff will send the face sheet, current medication list, physician and contact information, and advance directive or POLST information (RR-06) with the resident. The Administrator or designee will notify the person responsible for the resident and will contact the hospital within 24 hours to learn the status.

For any death, serious injury as determined by the physician, or incident threatening welfare, safety or health, the Administrator will submit a written report to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days (SAF-02, REC-02). Outbreaks, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents are reported by phone or fax to the licensing agency and the local health officer within 24 hours.

Before a resident returns from the hospital, the Administrator will obtain discharge orders and medication changes and will confirm that the resident's condition does not make a prohibited health condition apply and that the facility can safely meet the resident's needs. If the facility cannot meet the needs, the Administrator will follow ADM-06 and the notice rights described in the resident's admission agreement.

On the resident's return, the Administrator will update the medication record, perform a reappraisal and revise the service plan. The Administrator will explain any service or rate change to the resident and representative in writing, giving 60 days' written notice of rate changes as required by the admission agreement (RR-04).
The Administrator will inform the resident and representative that they may contact the licensing agency and the long-term care ombudsman about concerns relating to transfer or return (RR-03).
The Administrator will review each transfer within 5 business days for root causes and prevention opportunities and will document the review under GOV-05.

responsibilities.duty: Ensure physician and representative notification, reappraisal, service plan update, state reports, and readmission evaluation.
Carry out these duties when the Administrator is absent.
Observe, record and report changes the same shift, and call 9-1-1 for imminent threats.
Respond to calls, give orders, and provide discharge and follow-up instructions.
Support decisions about whether the facility can meet a resident's changed needs.

documentation: Daily notes recording observed changes
Physician contact log with date, time, person, instructions
Notification record for the person responsible
Hospital transfer packet checklist and transfer log
Written reports to licensing and proof of submission
Reappraisal and updated service plan
Readmission evaluation and discharge orders
Written notices of service or rate change
Transfer review notes

policies.title: Dementia and Memory Care
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Designated Substitute, all direct care and night staff, and any resident with dementia at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To provide safe, dignified care to residents with dementia, to meet staffing and training requirements, and to ensure any advertising of dementia care is supported by a written program.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides care to residents with dementia only to the extent staffing, training, environment and the individual service plan allow. Direct care staff complete required dementia training. If a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision, based on appraisal, reappraisal or observation, at least one night staff person is awake and on duty (in homes with fewer than 16 beds). If [AGENCY NAME] advertises dementia care, it maintains a written dementia program covering philosophy, admission, training, activities, environment, changes in condition and success indicators, and keeps its advertisements for 3 years. The plan of operation addresses how staff respond to residents' behavioral expressions, and staff are trained to recognize signs of dementia.

definitions.definition: A condition causing decline in memory, thinking and judgment that interferes with daily life, including Alzheimer's disease and related disorders.
A resident's behavior, such as agitation, wandering or repeated questions, that communicates an unmet need, discomfort or distress.
A staff person who is awake and on duty throughout the night, not merely on call.
The written description required of a facility that advertises dementia special care.

procedures: At pre-admission and every reappraisal, the Administrator will assess whether the resident shows signs of dementia, including memory loss, disorientation, wandering risk, and need for supervision, and will record whether awake night supervision is needed (ADM-01, ADM-02).

For homes with fewer than 16 beds, the Administrator will schedule at least one night staff person awake and on duty whenever a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision based on appraisal, reappraisal or observation. The Administrator will not admit or retain such a resident if awake night staff cannot be provided (see STF-01).
Night staff will know the emergency plan and will be trained in first aid, as required for night supervision, and will be oriented to residents who need awake supervision.

The Administrator will ensure that each direct care staff member completes dementia training: 12 hours initial and 8 hours annually. The first 20 hours of initial training, which must be completed before the staff member works alone, include 6 hours of dementia content. The second 20 hours, to be completed within 4 weeks, include 6 more hours, which together meet the 12-hour initial requirement. Annual training of 20 hours includes 8 hours on dementia.

Training will include recognizing signs of dementia, communication techniques, responding to behavioral expressions without force or restraint, wandering and elopement prevention, assisting with activities of daily living, and meaningful activities. The Administrator will keep trainer qualifications and attendance records in personnel files (STF-03, STF-05).
The Administrator will complete the dementia hours required for administrator continuing education and will keep proof in the Administrator's certification file (GOV-02).

The plan of operation will describe how staff respond to residents' behavioral expressions. Staff will first look for the cause of a behavior (pain, hunger, toileting needs, fear, noise, infection), use redirection and calm communication, and report patterns to the Administrator. Staff will not use restraints or restrictive practices except as permitted by SAF-04.

The service plan for each resident with dementia will describe the resident's routines, preferences, triggers, supervision level, wandering risk, communication needs and engagement activities (ADM-03). Staff will review the plan at hire and when it changes.

Staff will watch for changes in cognition or behavior, and will report them the same shift, because sudden change may indicate infection, medication effects or pain (HCS-05). The Administrator will seek physician evaluation.
The Administrator will implement wandering and elopement precautions per SAF-03, including a current photograph and description for each at-risk resident, and will review the environment for hazards.

The Administrator will provide structured, meaningful activities suited to residents with dementia daily (DL-02), and an environment that is safe, uncluttered and has good lighting and cues for orientation (DL-03).

If [AGENCY NAME] advertises dementia or memory care in any form, the Administrator will first adopt a written dementia program covering philosophy, admission criteria, staff training, activities, environment, changes in condition and indicators of success. The program will be available to prospective residents and licensing staff.

The Administrator will ensure every advertisement mentioning dementia care matches the written program and is accurate (GOV-06), and will keep a copy of each advertisement for 3 years from the date it was last used.

The Administrator will review the dementia program and each resident with dementia at least annually and whenever the facility's capabilities change, and will document the review under GOV-05. If a resident's needs exceed the facility's ability to meet them, the Administrator will follow ADM-04 and ADM-06.

responsibilities.duty: Approve the dementia program, fund staffing for awake night supervision, and ensure advertising is accurate.
Assess residents, schedule awake night staff, deliver and track training, maintain the written program and advertisements, and review annually.
Carry out these duties when the Administrator is absent.
Complete training, provide person-centered care, report changes, and maintain supervision.

Night staffing schedules showing awake staff
Dementia training records (hours, dates, trainer qualifications)
Administrator continuing education records
Service plans for residents with dementia
Written dementia program, if dementia care is advertised
Copies of advertisements kept for 3 years
Annual program review notes

policies.title: Falls Prevention
policies.applies_to: Administrator, Designated Substitute, direct care and maintenance staff, and all residents at [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To reduce the risk and severity of falls through observation, environmental safety, individualized planning and timely response and reporting.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] works to prevent falls and to respond promptly when they occur. The facility keeps the building safe, with non-slip surfaces, grab bars at toilets, tubs and showers, and emergency lighting, and observes residents for changes that increase fall risk. After any fall, staff provide first aid and call 9-1-1 for an imminent threat to health. The Administrator reappraises the resident when needed and updates the service plan. A serious injury under facility supervision, as determined by the physician, is reported in writing to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident within 7 days.

definitions.definition: An unplanned event in which a resident comes to rest on the floor, ground or other lower surface, whether or not injured.
An injury determined to be serious by the resident's physician.
Conditions that make falls more likely, such as unsteady gait, previous falls, medication side effects, poor vision, dizziness, footwear, clutter and poor lighting.
The resident's representative or family member identified in the admission agreement or appraisal.

procedures: At pre-admission appraisal and each reassessment, the Administrator will screen each resident for fall risk factors, including history of falls, gait and balance, vision, medications, continence needs, and cognition, and will record the findings (ADM-01, ADM-02).

The service plan will list fall prevention measures tailored to the resident, such as supervision level, assistance with transfers and walking, appropriate footwear, assistive devices, toileting schedule, and hydration (ADM-03). Staff will review plans at hire and when they change.

The Administrator or maintenance staff will inspect the building at least weekly for hazards: wet floors, loose rugs, clutter, uneven flooring, burned-out bulbs and blocked paths. Hazards are corrected immediately or the area is blocked off. Inspections are recorded on a log (DL-03).

The Administrator will ensure that walking and bathing surfaces are non-slip, that grab bars are installed and secure at toilets, tubs and showers, and that emergency lighting works. Bathrooms and bedrooms will meet the space and fixture standards for personal accommodations (no more than 2 residents per bedroom, and at least 1 toilet and washbasin per 6 persons and 1 tub or shower per 10, including live-in staff and family).

The Administrator will keep hot water between 105 and 120 degrees F and heat at 68 degrees F or above, so residents are not exposed to scald risk or cold that increases dizziness and stiffness. Plant maintenance will be kept up, and the Administrator will record temperature checks.

Staff will keep walkways, hallways and exits free of clutter, keep call devices or help methods within reach where used, and ensure that residents who use walkers, canes or wheelchairs have them nearby and in good repair.

Staff will observe residents daily for new unsteadiness, dizziness, weakness, new confusion or changes in vision or toileting, and will report them to the Administrator the same shift so that care can be adjusted and the physician notified (HCS-05).

When a resident falls, staff will not move the resident if serious injury is suspected. They will check responsiveness and look for injury, call 9-1-1 immediately for an imminent threat to health, give first aid within their training, and stay with the resident.

After any fall, staff will notify the Administrator or Designated Substitute the same shift. The Administrator will notify the resident's physician and the person responsible for the resident the same day, and will record the notifications.

Staff will complete a written incident report for each fall before the end of the shift, describing time, location, circumstances, injuries, footwear, witnesses, response and notifications (SAF-02). Staff will also observe the resident closely for delayed injury for at least 72 hours and record observations.

If the physician determines that the injury is serious, or if the fall is an incident threatening welfare, safety or health, the Administrator will submit a written report to the licensing agency and the person responsible within 7 days (REC-02).

Within 3 business days of a fall, the Administrator will review contributing factors, such as medications, environment, footwear, supervision and toileting, and will perform a reappraisal if the resident has fallen repeatedly or has had a change in condition (ADM-02). The Administrator will update the service plan and arrange physical therapy or other evaluation through a licensed professional if needed (HCS-04).
The Administrator will review all falls monthly for patterns by time, location, staff and resident, will implement corrective action and will document the review under GOV-05.
The Administrator will train staff at orientation and annually on fall prevention, safe transfers, and responding to falls (STF-03).

responsibilities.duty: Assess fall risk, maintain a safe environment, ensure incident reports and state reports, and review fall trends.
Carry out these duties when the Administrator is absent.
Follow service plan fall measures, remove hazards, respond to falls, and report promptly.
Inspect and repair floors, lighting, grab bars and water temperature.
Evaluate injuries and determine whether an injury is serious.

Water temperature and heat check records

policies.title: Skin Integrity and Pressure Injuries
policies.applies_to: All direct care staff, the Administrator and designated substitute, and all residents of [AGENCY NAME] (Residential Care Facility for the Elderly, California).
policies.purpose: To protect residents' skin, to find skin breakdown early, and to make sure [AGENCY NAME] does not admit or keep a resident with a condition the state prohibits, specifically stage 3 or stage 4 pressure injuries.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides personal care that helps prevent skin breakdown and responds promptly to any change in a resident's skin. Under 22 CCR §87615, a resident who needs health services for, or who has, a stage 3 or stage 4 pressure injury cannot be admitted or retained. Staff observe and report skin changes, and do not assess, stage or treat wounds. Wound assessment and treatment are done by licensed professionals such as a physician or a home health agency, within the limits in HCS-04. A resident with a stage 1 or stage 2 injury or another healing wound is considered for admission or retention only as allowed under ADM-05 and the Department's restricted health condition requirements. Residents have the right to appropriate care that does not cause avoidable discomfort. Staff respect this right in every part of skin care and repositioning.

definitions.definition: Localized damage to the skin or underlying tissue, usually over a bony area, caused by pressure or pressure combined with shear or friction. Also called a pressure ulcer, bedsore or decubitus ulcer.

A deep pressure injury, as staged by a licensed health professional, involving full-thickness skin loss or damage reaching fat, muscle or bone. These are prohibited health conditions under 22 CCR §87615.
Any new or worsening redness that does not fade, blister, open area, bruise, swelling, warmth, drainage, odor, pain or discoloration.
A physician, registered nurse or other licensed health professional, including one employed by a home health agency, who is legally permitted to assess and treat wounds.

procedures: Before admission, the Administrator or designee reviews the physician's report and the pre-admission appraisal (ADM-01) for any pressure injury, open wound or history of skin breakdown, and documents the finding.

If the appraisal or physician's report shows a stage 3 or stage 4 pressure injury, or a need for health services for one, the Administrator declines admission and tells the applicant or representative the reason in writing.

If the appraisal shows a stage 1 or stage 2 injury or other healing wound, the Administrator evaluates it under ADM-05 and does not admit unless those requirements are met and care can be provided safely, including by a licensed professional as needed.
Care staff look at each resident's skin during bathing, dressing and toileting. Staff are trained in personal care, including bathing and toileting, under STF-03.
Staff report any skin change to the Administrator or designee before the end of the shift, and sooner if the area is open, draining or painful. The report is recorded in the resident's daily notes.

Staff use prevention measures in the service plan: prompt incontinence care, keeping skin clean and dry, offering position changes to residents who sit or lie for long periods, and encouraging fluids and meals (DL-01).
Positioning devices, cushions or other supports are used only as ordered by the physician and consistent with SAF-04 and the resident's service plan.

When a skin change is found, the Administrator or designee notifies the resident's physician and the responsible person, and arranges evaluation by the physician or a home health agency. The notice and its date and time are documented.
Only a licensed professional stages a pressure injury and performs wound assessment, dressing changes and treatment. Facility staff do not perform tasks outside the limits in HCS-04.

Staff follow the physician's or home health agency's written instructions for care that staff are permitted to do, such as repositioning prompts, keeping the area clean and dry, and reporting. Staff document each task done.

If a licensed professional stages a pressure injury as stage 3 or stage 4, the Administrator immediately notifies the physician and the responsible person, and begins the relocation process under ADM-04 and ADM-06. The Administrator documents the date of diagnosis and every step taken.
The Administrator updates the resident's reassessment (ADM-02) and individualized service plan (ADM-03) after any skin change, and reports significant changes under HCS-05.

If a resident refuses repositioning, bathing or treatment, staff respect the refusal, offer alternatives, notify the Administrator, and document the refusal. The Administrator informs the physician and the responsible person.

If a skin injury appears unexplained or suggests neglect or abuse, staff report it immediately to the Administrator and follow SAF-01. If the physician determines the injury is serious, the Administrator follows SAF-02.
The Administrator reviews skin-related events at least quarterly as part of internal compliance review (GOV-05) and corrects any gaps in training or practice.

responsibilities.duty: Screens applicants for prohibited conditions, decides on admission and retention, arranges physician and home health evaluation, starts relocation when a prohibited condition arises, and keeps records.
Observe skin during personal care, carry out prevention measures in the service plan, report skin changes before end of shift, and document care and refusals.

responsibilities.role: Licensed professional (physician or home health agency)
responsibilities.duty: Assess and stage injuries, provide wound treatment, and give written instructions to the facility.
Carries out the Administrator's duties in this policy when the Administrator is absent.

policies.title: Hospice and Home Health Coordination
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, designated substitute, direct care staff, and all residents who receive hospice or home health services at [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure residents receive hospice and home health services safely and legally, that the facility holds the required hospice care waiver, and that facility staff and outside agencies coordinate care clearly.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] allows a resident who is terminally ill to remain in the facility with hospice services only if the facility has an approved hospice care waiver from CDSS and the resident's needs can be met. Under 22 CCR §87632, the facility submits a written request that states the maximum number of hospice residents, and CDSS decides within 30 days of an acceptable request. Facility staff do not provide nursing or hospice services themselves. Those services are provided by the hospice or home health agency, within the limits in HCS-04. The facility coordinates with the agency, keeps the plan of care in the resident's record, includes hospice residents in its disaster plan, and handles a hospice resident's medications according to the hospice agency's procedures. Direct care staff receive training that includes 4 hours on postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice (HSC §1569.625).

definitions.definition: Written approval from CDSS Community Care Licensing allowing the facility to care for residents receiving hospice services, up to the maximum number of hospice residents stated in the request (22 CCR §87632).
A licensed agency that provides palliative and supportive services to a terminally ill resident and the resident's family.
A licensed agency that provides skilled nursing, therapy or other health services to a resident in the facility on a physician's order.
The resident's representative, conservator, agent under an advance directive or other person identified in the admission agreement.

procedures: Before accepting any hospice resident, the Administrator confirms that the facility's hospice care waiver is approved. If it is not, the Administrator submits a written request to CDSS stating the maximum number of hospice residents the facility will serve. CDSS decides within 30 days of an acceptable request.
The Administrator keeps the approved waiver on file, never exceeds the maximum number of hospice residents it allows, and sends a new written request if the facility wants to change that number.
When a resident or responsible person asks for hospice, the Administrator meets with them and the hospice agency to review the resident's needs and decide whether the facility can safely meet them.
The Administrator obtains the hospice agency's name, contact numbers, 24-hour on-call number, the physician's order for hospice and the hospice plan of care, and places them in the resident's record.

The Administrator updates the resident's reassessment (ADM-02) and individualized service plan (ADM-03) to show who provides which services. The hospice or home health agency provides nursing and hospice services. Facility staff provide personal care, meals, supervision and help with self-administered medications as allowed.
Staff do not perform nursing tasks outside the limits in HCS-04. If a task is outside those limits, the Administrator asks the hospice or home health agency to perform it.

Staff follow the resident's advance directive and any POLST (RR-06). Staff know how to reach the hospice agency's on-call line and call it promptly with any change in condition, in addition to the steps in HCS-05.
The Administrator or designee communicates with the hospice agency at each visit and records any new orders, equipment, supplies and changes in the care plan.

Medications for a hospice resident are stored and assisted with under HCS-01 and HCS-02, using the original container and the physician's or hospice's order. Staff may not give injections unless authorized by law.

When a hospice resident's medication is no longer needed or the resident dies, the facility disposes of it according to the hospice agency's procedures. The disposal is recorded, and the record is kept as required for medication destruction under 22 CCR §87465.

The facility's disaster plan (SAF-05) lists each hospice resident. If the facility evacuates or relocates, the Administrator or designee notifies the resident's hospice agency, as required by 22 CCR §87212, and documents the call.

All direct care staff complete the required training that includes 4 hours on postural supports, restricted conditions and hospice (HSC §1569.625). The Administrator records completion in the personnel file (STF-03, STF-05).
The facility coordinates home health agency visits in the same way: it obtains orders and visit notes, notifies the agency of changes, and keeps records in the resident's file.

If the resident's needs exceed what the facility can safely provide, or the facility's waiver limit would be exceeded, the Administrator discusses options with the resident, responsible person and hospice agency. Any move or discharge follows ADM-06.
When a hospice resident dies, the Administrator follows HCS-10 and tells the hospice agency right away.

responsibilities.duty: Obtains and maintains the hospice care waiver, decides whether the facility can meet the resident's needs, coordinates with agencies, and ensures records and training are in place.
Provide personal care and supervision per the service plan, report changes to the Administrator and the hospice agency, and follow instructions of licensed professionals.
Provide nursing, hospice and other skilled services, issue written orders and care plans, and direct disposal of hospice medications.
Coordinates with the hospice agency when the Administrator is absent.

policies.title: Death of a Resident
policies.applies_to: The Administrator, designated substitute and all staff of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure a resident's death is handled with dignity, that required reports are made on time, that fees, property and medications are properly handled, and that records are updated.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] treats every resident's death with respect and notifies the family and responsible person promptly. The death of any resident, from any cause and wherever it occurs, including in a hospital, in transit or away from the facility, is reported in writing to the licensing agency and to the person responsible for the resident within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). The facility refunds prepaid fees as stated in the admission agreement and state law, and gives written notice to the payor when the payor is not the responsible person (22 CCR §87507). Unreturned medications are destroyed with a two-signature record kept for 3 years (22 CCR §87465). The register of residents is updated.

definitions.definition: The resident's representative, conservator, agent under an advance directive or other person named in the admission agreement.
The CDSS Community Care Licensing Division, Adult and Senior Care Program, through the regional office that oversees the facility.
A person or agency, other than the resident or the responsible person, who pays for the resident's care.
A record of medication destruction signed by the Administrator and one other adult who is not a resident.

procedures: When staff find a resident unresponsive or not breathing, they follow the resident's advance directive or POLST (RR-06) and call 9-1-1 as that document and the facility's emergency procedures require. Staff immediately notify the Administrator or designated substitute.
The Administrator or designee notifies the resident's physician and, as required by law, the county coroner or law enforcement, and follows their directions on the body and the scene.

The Administrator or designee promptly notifies the responsible person and family, and the hospice agency if the resident was receiving hospice (HCS-09). The calls are recorded with date, time and the person reached.
Staff protect privacy and dignity: they close the resident's door, limit entry, and inform other residents with compassion and in a manner suited to their understanding.
If the death is unexpected, unexplained or possibly related to abuse, neglect or an accident, the Administrator also follows SAF-01 and SAF-02 and preserves the scene as directed by authorities.

The Administrator makes sure the resident's body is released only to the funeral home or other party designated by the responsible person or authorized by the coroner, and records the time, the name of the party and who released the body.

Within 7 days of the death, the Administrator submits a written report to the licensing agency and sends a copy to the person responsible for the resident. The report includes the resident's name, age, sex and date of admission; the date and nature of the event; the attending physician's name, findings and treatment; and the disposition. This applies even if the death occurred away from the facility.
The Administrator keeps a copy of the report and proof of delivery in the resident's record and the facility's incident file (SAF-02).
Personal property and valuables are inventoried by two staff members and secured. They are released to the responsible person or legal representative following RR-05, with signed receipts.

The Administrator reviews the admission agreement and calculates any refund of prepaid fees owed under its terms and state law. The Administrator gives written notice to the payor if the payor is different from the responsible person, and issues any refund promptly, with an itemized statement, as the agreement requires (RR-04).

Medications belonging to the resident that are not returned to the family are destroyed by the Administrator and one other adult who is not a resident, using the two-signature log. The log is kept for at least 3 years. A hospice resident's medications are disposed of according to the hospice agency's procedures.
The Administrator updates the register of residents to show the date of death and removes the resident from active census (REC-01).
Staff clean and prepare the room under SAF-07 and DL-03, and the Administrator checks that no resident has been left without needed support after the loss of a roommate.
The Administrator offers the family and affected residents and staff an opportunity to talk about the loss, and may offer a memorial gathering with the family's consent.
The resident's record is closed and kept for the period required in REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Directs the response, notifies family and agencies, files the 7-day written report, handles refunds and property, destroys medications, and updates the register.
Takes on these duties when the Administrator is absent.
Call 9-1-1 and the Administrator as required, protect the resident's dignity and privacy, and help secure belongings.
Carries out its role at the time of death and directs disposal of hospice medications.

documentation: Written report to licensing and the responsible person with proof of delivery
Notification log with date, time and names
Incident notes
Property inventory and release receipts
Refund calculation and notice to payor
Two-signature medication destruction log (kept at least 3 years)
Updated register of residents
Release record for the body

policies.title: Abuse, Neglect and Exploitation Prevention and Reporting
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers, the Administrator and the governing body of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To protect residents from abuse, neglect and exploitation, and to make sure all suspected abuse is reported to the right agencies within the required time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not tolerate abuse, neglect or exploitation of any resident. Residents have the right to be free from punishment, humiliation, intimidation and abuse (22 CCR §87468.1). All facility staff are mandated reporters under Welfare and Institutions Code §15630. Staff report suspected abuse of an elder or dependent adult by phone immediately or as soon as practicably possible, followed by a written report on form SOC 341. For suspected physical abuse, the facility reports to the local ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement within 2 hours if the abuse results in serious bodily injury, and otherwise within 24 hours (22 CCR §87211(b),(c)). Psychological abuse by staff or residents, and any incident threatening a resident's welfare, safety or health, is reported in writing to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). No staff member or volunteer works or is present in the facility without criminal record clearance or an exemption (22 CCR §87355). If [AGENCY NAME] participates in the Medi-Cal Assisted Living Waiver, it also follows the federal rights and settings requirements at 42 CFR 441.301(c) (see GOV-08).

definitions.definition: A person required by law, including care custodians and facility staff, to report suspected abuse of an elder or dependent adult.

Includes physical abuse, psychological or emotional abuse, sexual abuse, neglect, financial exploitation, abandonment, isolation and abduction, as described in Welfare and Institutions Code §15630 and related law.

An injury involving a substantial risk of death, unconsciousness, extreme physical pain, protracted loss or impairment of a body part or function, or requiring medical intervention such as surgery, hospitalization or rehabilitation.
The state form used to make the written report of suspected elder or dependent adult abuse.
The local Long-Term Care Ombudsman program, part of the California Department of Aging, which advocates for residents and receives mandated abuse reports.

procedures: Before any person starts work or is present in the facility, the Administrator confirms DOJ and FBI fingerprint criminal record clearance or an exemption under STF-02. No one works or is present without it.

The Administrator trains all new staff on this policy at orientation and refreshes the training at least annually (STF-03). Staff sign that they understand they are mandated reporters and that they may not delay or avoid reporting.

The facility posts the Long-Term Care Ombudsman CRISISline, 1-800-231-4024, along with the local ombudsman number [LOCAL OMBUDSMAN PHONE] and the licensing agency number [LICENSING REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE] where residents and visitors can see them (RR-03).

Any staff member who sees, suspects or is told about abuse, neglect or exploitation acts at once to protect the resident, separates the resident from the alleged abuser, and gets medical care if needed, calling 9-1-1 in an emergency.

The staff member who witnessed or suspects the abuse reports it personally. A mandated reporter does not need approval from the Administrator and does not wait for the Administrator before making the required report. The staff member also tells the Administrator or designated substitute as soon as possible.

For suspected physical abuse that results in serious bodily injury, the report is made by phone to the local ombudsman, the licensing agency and local law enforcement within 2 hours. For suspected physical abuse without serious bodily injury, the report is made to the same three agencies within 24 hours (22 CCR §87211(b),(c)).

For any other suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, including financial abuse and abuse by a resident, the staff member or Administrator makes the phone report immediately or as soon as practicably possible as Welfare and Institutions Code §15630 requires, and follows with a written report.
The reporter completes and sends form SOC 341 in writing within the time the statute requires. The Administrator reviews the written report to make sure it was sent.

For psychological abuse by staff or residents, and any incident threatening welfare, safety or health, the Administrator sends a written report to the licensing agency and to the person responsible for the resident within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). See also SAF-02.
The Administrator notifies the resident's responsible person and physician promptly, and arranges medical care and emotional support. The Administrator documents each notification.

The Administrator protects the resident and others while the matter is reviewed. A staff member accused of abuse is removed from contact with residents pending review. Evidence is preserved, and staff and residents are not discouraged from speaking with investigators.
The facility cooperates fully with law enforcement, the ombudsman and licensing, and gives them access to residents and records as the law allows (RR-03).
No one is punished or retaliated against for reporting in good faith, whether a resident, family member or staff member. Retaliation is grounds for discipline up to termination (STF-06).

After each report, the Administrator reviews what happened, updates the resident's service plan if needed, and corrects any staffing, training or environmental causes. The governing body is informed (GOV-01, GOV-05).
The Administrator keeps all abuse reports, proof of submission and follow-up in a confidential incident file, separate from the resident's routine record.

responsibilities.duty: Protect residents, report suspected abuse immediately as mandated reporters, and cooperate with investigations.
Ensures clearances, training and postings are current, checks that all required reports are made on time, protects residents, and corrects causes.
Receives reports and ensures timely reporting when the Administrator is absent.
Receives reports of abuse incidents and ensures corrective action (GOV-01).

documentation: Completed SOC 341 forms and proof of submission
Phone report log with date, time, agency and person contacted
7-day written reports to licensing and the responsible person
Criminal record clearance or exemption records
Staff mandated reporter acknowledgements and training records
Incident investigation notes and corrective action
Photo of posted ombudsman and licensing numbers

policies.title: Incident, Accident and Unusual Incident Reporting
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator and designated substitute of [AGENCY NAME].
policies.purpose: To make sure every incident, accident and unusual occurrence is responded to, recorded and reported to the licensing agency, local authorities and the responsible person within the times California requires.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] reports incidents as required by 22 CCR §87211. A written report is sent to the licensing agency and to the person responsible for the resident within 7 days for any death, any serious injury as determined by the physician, any use of an automated external defibrillator (AED), and any incident that threatens the welfare, safety or health of a resident. Epidemic outbreaks, poisonings, catastrophes and major accidents are reported within 24 hours by phone or fax to the licensing agency and, when appropriate, the local health officer. Fires and explosions are reported immediately to the local fire authority and no later than the next working day to the licensing agency. Staff call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to a resident's health (22 CCR §87465).

definitions.definition: An event listed in 22 CCR §87211: death, serious injury as determined by the physician, AED use, or any incident threatening welfare, safety or health, including unexplained absence and psychological abuse.
An injury that the resident's physician determines to be serious.
The resident's representative, conservator, agent or other person named in the admission agreement.
The public health official for the county or city in which the facility is located.

procedures: Staff who see or learn of an incident, accident or unusual occurrence first make the resident and others safe. They provide first aid within staff training and call 9-1-1 for any imminent threat to health (22 CCR §87465).
Staff notify the Administrator or designated substitute immediately by phone, whatever the hour.
The Administrator or designee calls the resident's physician and the responsible person right away for any injury, illness, or significant event, and records the time and the person reached (HCS-05).
The staff member who witnessed or discovered the event writes an incident report before the end of the shift, describing what was seen and done in factual terms, without opinions.

The Administrator decides whether the event is reportable under 22 CCR §87211 and records the decision, using the list in this policy. If unsure, the Administrator calls the licensing agency at [LICENSING REGIONAL OFFICE PHONE] and reports.

For a death, a serious injury as determined by the physician, any AED use, or any incident threatening welfare, safety or health (including unexplained absence and psychological abuse), the Administrator submits a written report to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident within 7 days.

For an epidemic outbreak, poisoning, catastrophe or major accident, the Administrator reports by phone or fax to the licensing agency within 24 hours and, when appropriate, to the local health officer at [LOCAL HEALTH OFFICER PHONE].

For a fire or explosion, the Administrator or staff on duty notify the local fire authority immediately, and the Administrator notifies the licensing agency no later than the next working day. Fire response follows SAF-06.
Each written report includes the resident's name, age, sex and date of admission; the date and nature of the event; the physician's findings and treatment; and the disposition of the resident.

If an incident involves suspected abuse, neglect or exploitation, the Administrator also follows the faster timelines in SAF-01. If it involves a missing resident, SAF-03 applies. A death follows HCS-10.
The Administrator keeps the original report, proof of submission to the licensing agency, and a copy of the notification to the responsible person together in the incident file.
The Administrator reviews each incident within [NUMBER] days to find causes, updates the resident's service plan (ADM-03) and corrects hazards, staffing or training problems.
The Administrator reviews all incident reports at least quarterly for patterns such as repeated falls, medication errors or elopement, and records actions taken (GOV-05).
Incident files are kept in the facility and made available to licensing on request, as set out in REC-01.

responsibilities.duty: Make residents safe, call 9-1-1 when needed, notify the Administrator immediately, and write a factual incident report before end of shift.
Determines reportability, makes all agency and family notifications on time, keeps the incident file, and directs corrective action.
Makes the notifications and reports when the Administrator is absent.

documentation: Staff incident reports
Written 7-day reports to licensing and the responsible person
Records of 24-hour phone or fax reports and next-working-day fire reports
Notification log for physician and responsible person
Corrective action notes
Quarterly incident trend review

policies.title: Elopement, Unexplained Absence and Missing Resident
policies.applies_to: All staff, the Administrator and designated substitute of [AGENCY NAME], with special attention to residents with dementia or cognitive impairment.
policies.purpose: To respect residents' right to come and go while responding quickly and effectively when a resident is missing or leaves unexpectedly and may be at risk.
policies.policy: Residents may leave the facility at any time and cannot be locked in (22 CCR §87468.1). Locking doors at night or barring windows requires permission from the Department. [AGENCY NAME] manages wandering risk through appraisal, service planning, supervision and environmental safety rather than by confinement. An unexplained absence of any resident is a reportable incident, and a written report is sent to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)). Staff call 9-1-1 if the absence creates an imminent threat to the resident's health (22 CCR §87465). Where a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision, at least one night staff person is awake and on duty in homes with fewer than 16 beds (22 CCR §87705). The search and notification steps below are the facility's own, because the state has not prescribed specific search steps.

definitions.definition: A resident with cognitive impairment or at risk of harm leaving the facility or its grounds without staff knowledge, or in a way that places the resident at risk.
A resident cannot be located and no one knows where the resident is, or the resident has not returned when expected and the reason is unknown.
A resident who has signed out or whose whereabouts are known and agreed, such as a family outing.
At least one staff person awake and on duty through the night when a resident needs it, based on appraisal, reappraisal or observation.

procedures: At pre-admission appraisal and each reassessment (ADM-01, ADM-02), the Administrator identifies residents who are at risk of wandering or leaving, such as those with dementia, and records the risk level and supervision needed.

The service plan (ADM-03) states the supervision, activities and interventions for each at-risk resident. Interventions never include locking a resident in or any restraint. Any door alarm or similar device is reviewed against SAF-04 and resident rights.
