When a resident has dementia and needs awake night supervision, the Administrator schedules at least one awake night staff person every night, as required in homes with fewer than 16 beds (22 CCR §87705; STF-01, HCS-06).
Residents who go out on their own or with family use a sign-out and sign-in system showing destination and expected return time. A resident who is out on an agreed outing is not a missing resident.
Any staff member who cannot find a resident, or sees a resident leaving who may be at risk, immediately tells the Administrator or designated substitute, and begins searching without delay.

Staff on duty immediately do a head count of all residents, check the resident's room, bathrooms, common areas, outdoor areas, garage, vehicles and nearby places, and ask other staff and residents. Another staff member continues to care for the remaining residents.

If the resident is not found in [NUMBER] minutes, or at once if the resident has dementia, is frail, or is in danger because of weather, traffic or health conditions, staff call 9-1-1 and give the resident's description, clothing, medical conditions and last known location. This is required if the absence creates an imminent threat to health (22 CCR §87465).
The Administrator or designee notifies the responsible person and the resident's physician as soon as the resident is considered missing, and tells them the steps taken. The notification is recorded.
Staff keep a current photo and physical description in the resident's file so that law enforcement can be given them immediately.

When the resident is found, staff check the resident for injury, call the physician or 9-1-1 as needed, tell the responsible person and any agencies called that the resident has been found, and make sure the resident is comfortable and safe.

The Administrator sends a written report of the unexplained absence to the licensing agency and the person responsible for the resident within 7 days (22 CCR §87211(a)(1)), and follows SAF-02 for the incident file. If the resident was hurt or abuse or neglect is suspected, SAF-01 also applies.

The Administrator reviews how the event happened, including whether supervision, alarms, staffing or doors failed, and updates the service plan, staffing and environmental safety. The Administrator may reassess whether the facility can continue to meet the resident's needs (ADM-04).
Staff are trained on this policy at orientation and refresher training (STF-03). The Administrator holds a missing-resident drill at least [NUMBER] times a year and records it.
The Administrator reviews all missing-resident events quarterly as part of internal compliance review (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Identifies wandering risk, plans supervision and night staffing, directs the search, makes all notifications and reports, and corrects causes.
Directs the search and notifications when the Administrator is absent.
Supervise residents per the service plan, start searching immediately when a resident is missing, call for help and document.
Remain awake and on duty at night when a resident needs awake supervision, and respond immediately to alarms or noises.

documentation: Risk findings in the pre-admission appraisal and reassessments
Service plan interventions for wandering risk
Sign-out and sign-in log
Missing resident incident report, with times of each step
Records of 9-1-1 call and notifications to responsible person and physician
Written 7-day report to licensing and the responsible person
Drill records
Post-event review and corrective action

policies.title: Restraints, Postural Supports and Restrictive Practices
policies.applies_to: All staff, administrator, designated substitute, volunteers and contracted providers at [AGENCY NAME] (California RCFE)
federal: 42 CFR 441.301(c) (HCBS modifications must be documented, if ALW)
policies.purpose: To protect residents from restraint, seclusion, confinement, punishment and intimidation, and to make sure any postural support is used only as California Title 22 allows, with the required documentation and trained staff.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] does not use physical restraint, chemical restraint, seclusion or locked confinement on any resident. Under 22 CCR §87468.1, residents have the right to be free from punishment, humiliation, intimidation and abuse, and from interference with eating, sleeping or elimination. They also have the right to leave at any time and not be locked into any room, building or premises. Staff never hide, camouflage or force medications. A postural support is used only when it is permitted under the Title 22 postural-support regulations, is documented as those regulations require, and is used by staff who completed postural-support training under HSC §1569.625. If ALW participation applies, any modification of a resident's rights is also documented in the service plan as federal HCBS rules require. Any practice that restricts a resident's movement, access or choices that is not covered by this policy must be approved in advance by the Administrator and checked against Title 22 before use.

definitions.definition: Any manual method, device or equipment that the resident cannot easily remove and that limits free movement or normal access to the body. [AGENCY NAME] prohibits this.

A device used to achieve proper body position and balance or to improve a resident's functioning, used only as permitted by the Title 22 postural-support regulations and never as a means of restraint or staff convenience.
Use of a medication, or concealing or forcing a medication, to control behavior or restrict movement rather than to treat a physician-diagnosed condition. This is prohibited.
Involuntarily confining a resident to a room or area, or locking a resident into a room, building or premises. This is prohibited.
Any rule, device or action that limits a resident's rights, movement, access to food, visitors or belongings.

procedures: The Administrator reviews this policy with every new employee during orientation, before the employee works alone, and documents it in the personnel record.

Direct care staff complete the 4 hours of postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice training that HSC §1569.625 requires within the first 20 hours of initial training, before working alone. The Administrator records the date, trainer and hours in the personnel file.

Staff never tie, hold down, bind or otherwise restrain a resident, and never use sheets, belts, straps, geri-chairs with locked trays, bed rails or similar devices to keep a resident in place unless the Administrator has confirmed the device is an allowed postural support under Title 22.

Before any postural support is considered, the Administrator or designee, with the resident's physician, resident and representative, documents the medical symptom or need and the less restrictive alternatives tried, such as repositioning, a different chair, supervision, toileting schedule or physical therapy review.

No postural support is applied until the Administrator has verified that all documentation required by the Title 22 postural-support regulations is complete. This includes the physician's order and any required consent. The Administrator attaches it to the resident's record and updates the Individualized Service Plan (ADM-03).

Staff apply and remove an approved postural support only as the order and the manufacturer's directions say. They check the resident's position, skin and comfort at the intervals set in the order and the service plan, and never leave a resident unobserved in a support that cannot be released.

Staff record each use, any skin or comfort problem, and each check in the resident's record. The Administrator reviews the use at least with each reassessment (ADM-02) and whenever the resident's condition changes.
The Administrator discontinues a postural support as soon as it is no longer needed or the physician withdraws the order, and documents the date and reason.

No door, gate or window is locked in a way that prevents a resident from leaving. Any door alarm, wander-prevention system or secured area for memory care must be reviewed by the Administrator against Title 22 and the fire clearance and approved by licensing before use (see HCS-06, SAF-03 and SAF-06).
Staff never withhold or interfere with food, sleep, toileting, visitors, phone or mail as punishment or for staff convenience.

Staff never hide medication in food or drink, crush or disguise medication, or force a resident to take it. A resident who refuses a medication is documented as refusing, the physician or authorized representative is notified, and the refusal is handled under HCS-02.

When a resident's behavior puts the resident or others at risk, staff use de-escalation: stay calm, reduce stimulation, offer choices, redirect and call the Administrator. If there is an imminent threat to health or safety, staff call 9-1-1 and do not physically restrain the resident.

The staff member reports any suspected restraint, confinement, punishment or intimidation to the Administrator immediately. The Administrator treats it as possible abuse and follows SAF-01 and SAF-02, including the required reports.

Any restriction on an ALW resident's rights, such as access to food, visitors or the community, is permitted only if documented in the service plan with the assessed need, less intrusive methods tried, time limits, review schedule and the resident's informed consent, as federal HCBS rules require.
The Administrator reviews all postural-support use, behavior incidents and reports of restraint or confinement quarterly under GOV-05, and corrects practices or retrains staff as needed.

responsibilities.duty: Prohibit restraint and confinement, verify Title 22 compliance and documentation before any postural support, train staff, review use at reassessment and quarterly, and report suspected violations.
Carry out this policy when the Administrator is absent and make no approval of a new restrictive practice.
Never restrain, lock in or punish a resident. Use postural supports only as ordered and trained. Document each use and report concerns immediately.
Evaluate the need for any postural support and issue and review the order.
Participate in decisions about postural supports and give any required consent.

documentation: Postural support documentation required by Title 22 (physician order, consent), kept in the resident record
Assessment of need and alternatives tried
Service plan updates
Application, check and discontinuation log
Staff training records showing the 4-hour postural supports topic
Incident and unusual incident reports for any restraint or confinement allegation
Quarterly review notes

policies.title: Emergency Preparedness and Disaster Plan
policies.applies_to: All staff, administrator, designated substitute, night staff and volunteers at [AGENCY NAME] (California RCFE)
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] has a written, current disaster and mass casualty plan that protects residents during fire, earthquake, flood, power loss, evacuation or other emergency, and that staff know their roles and report events to the state on time.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written disaster and mass casualty plan as 22 CCR §87212 requires. The plan is readily available to licensing and staff. It covers administrative authority and staff assignments; the fire safety plan; means of exiting; assembly at a predetermined evacuation site; transportation arrangements; relocation sites equipped for safe temporary accommodation; supervision of residents during evacuation and contact after relocation; contact with fire, law enforcement, civil defense and disaster authorities; and notification of a resident's hospice agency on evacuation or relocation. Emergency exit plans and emergency telephone numbers are posted. All staff, including night staff, know the plan. Catastrophes and major accidents are reported within 24 hours as 22 CCR §87211 requires.

definitions.definition: The written plan, submitted on the licensing agency's plan form (LIC 610E) with the application, that sets out how the facility will respond to events that threaten residents' safety.
The predetermined location near the facility where residents and staff assemble after leaving the building.
A site equipped for safe temporary accommodation of residents when they cannot return to the facility.
An event such as a disaster, serious structural or utility failure, or major accident that threatens resident welfare, safety or health and is reportable under 22 CCR §87211(a)(2).

procedures: Before licensure, the Administrator completes the written plan on LIC 610E, covering each element listed in §87212, and keeps it on site where staff and licensing can get it at once.

The Administrator assigns by name or position the emergency authority and each staff duty, such as calling 9-1-1, resident count, assisting nonambulatory residents, medications and records, and meeting responders. Assignments cover every shift, including nights and weekends, and are written in the plan.

The Administrator identifies the evacuation assembly site and one or more relocation sites, confirms their availability in writing with the owner or manager, and records addresses, contacts and capacity [EVACUATION SITE] [RELOCATION SITE].

The Administrator arranges transportation for evacuation and relocation, including for residents who use wheelchairs or need assistance, and records who is responsible for vehicles, drivers and accessible transport.

The Administrator posts the emergency exit plan and a list of emergency telephone numbers in a visible place. The list includes 9-1-1, fire, law enforcement, ambulance, poison control, the local health officer, the licensing agency, the Ombudsman, the Administrator and the utilities. Ambulance numbers are also kept where staff can get them quickly, as 22 CCR §87465 requires.

The Administrator keeps current a resident roster with each resident's mobility, medications, diagnoses, physician, hospice agency if any, and responsible person's phone number. A copy goes with staff during evacuation.
The Administrator maintains emergency supplies, including a first aid kit, flashlights, water, food, medications supply plan and resident records access, in amounts set in the plan.

The Administrator orients each new employee to the plan, exits, assembly site, emergency numbers and their assignments before the employee works alone. Night staff receive and document this training before working any night shift.

At least as often as the plan and fire authority require, the Administrator conducts emergency drills for all shifts, reviews how long evacuation took and any problems, and corrects deficiencies. Fire drills are also governed by SAF-06.

In any emergency, the senior staff member calls 9-1-1 first for an imminent threat to health or safety, then notifies the Administrator, and begins the actions assigned in the plan. Staff protect residents first and do not return to a hazardous building.

If evacuation is ordered or necessary, staff move residents to the assembly site, take a count against the roster, bring medications and records if safe, supervise residents continuously, and move them to the relocation site if they cannot return.

When residents are evacuated or relocated, the Administrator or designee notifies each resident's hospice agency, physician and responsible person. The Administrator keeps contact with residents and the relocation site as the plan describes.

The Administrator reports any catastrophe or major accident to the licensing agency and the local health officer within 24 hours by phone or fax. A fire or explosion is reported immediately to the local fire authority and no later than the next working day to licensing (SAF-06). A written report of any incident threatening resident welfare, safety or health goes to licensing and the person responsible for each affected resident within 7 days (SAF-02, REC-02).
After any actual emergency or drill, the Administrator holds a debriefing, documents lessons learned and updates the plan.

The Administrator reviews the plan at least annually, whenever the building, residents' needs, sites or contacts change, and after any emergency, and records the date and changes in the plan's revision log (GOV-04).

responsibilities.duty: Write, post, keep current and train staff on the plan, arrange sites and transport, run drills, make required reports and conduct reviews.
Take emergency authority when the Administrator is absent and follow the plan.
Know the plan, exits, assembly site and assignments, and carry out assigned duties.
Know the plan and be able to evacuate residents with the staffing present, and call for help immediately.

documentation: Written disaster and mass casualty plan (LIC 610E) with revision log
Posted exit plans and telephone list
Evacuation and relocation site agreements
Drill records and debriefing notes
Staff orientation and training records
Resident roster with emergency information
Reports to licensing and local health officer
Emergency supply checklist

policies.title: Fire Safety, Clearance, Evacuation and Drills
policies.applies_to: Administrator, designated substitute, all staff and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME] (California RCFE)
policies.purpose: To make sure the facility holds the required fire clearances, maintains fire safety, and that staff can evacuate every resident, including those who cannot walk, in a fire.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] holds a fire clearance from the local fire authority before licensure, as 22 CCR §87202 requires. It obtains a separate fire clearance before accepting or keeping any nonambulatory or bedridden resident. The fire safety plan and means of exiting are part of the disaster plan (22 CCR §87212). Fires and explosions are reported immediately to the local fire authority and no later than the next working day to licensing (22 CCR §87211). The facility follows the Title 22 fire safety and capacity and ambulatory-limit rules and the directions of the fire authority, and keeps equipment inspected and exits clear.

definitions.definition: Approval issued by the local fire authority or State Fire Marshal that the facility meets fire safety requirements for its use and resident population.
A resident who cannot leave the building without assistance in an emergency or who is confined to a bed. These residents require a separate fire clearance (see ADM-05).
A practice evacuation that tests staff response, exits and the time needed to move residents to safety.
The unobstructed route from every room to the outside, including doors, hallways, ramps and exits.

procedures: Before applying for licensure, the Administrator requests a fire clearance inspection from the local fire authority, provides requested information on capacity and resident types, and corrects every item the inspector cites. The fire clearance is filed in the licensing file and with the application (GOV-03).
The Administrator does not admit a resident beyond the capacity and ambulatory status that the fire clearance and license allow.

Before accepting or keeping a nonambulatory or bedridden resident, the Administrator confirms with licensing and the fire authority that the separate fire clearance is in place and files a copy. If not, the resident is not admitted or retained, and ADM-04, ADM-05 and ADM-06 are followed.
The Administrator writes the fire safety plan and exit routes into the disaster plan (SAF-05), posts exit diagrams, and assigns each staff member's fire duties for every shift.

The Administrator sets up and records an inspection and testing schedule for smoke alarms, fire extinguishers, any sprinklers, alarm system, emergency lighting and other fire equipment according to the fire authority's requirements and manufacturer directions. Defects are fixed promptly and recorded.

Staff check exits, hallways, stairs and doors every shift to confirm they are unobstructed and operable from the inside. Blocked or locked exits are corrected at once. Furniture, equipment and storage are never allowed to block exit routes.

The Administrator conducts fire drills on every shift, including nights, at the frequency required by the fire authority and Title 22 and set in the fire safety plan [DRILL SCHEDULE]. Residents participate to the extent safe, and the drill includes moving residents who need assistance.
After each drill, the Administrator records the date, time, shift, staff present, evacuation time, residents assisted, problems and corrections, and signs the record.

During a fire, staff follow the posted plan: rescue residents in immediate danger if safe, activate the alarm, call 9-1-1, close doors, evacuate residents to the assembly site, count against the roster and keep residents supervised until released.
Staff do not use elevators for evacuation and do not re-enter the building until the fire authority permits.

The Administrator reports a fire or explosion immediately to the local fire authority and no later than the next working day to the licensing agency. The report is then followed with a written report within 7 days if a death, injury or other reportable event occurred (SAF-02, REC-02).

After a fire, the Administrator notifies each resident's responsible person, physician and hospice agency if any, arranges relocation if needed (SAF-05), and does not resume use of damaged areas until the fire authority and licensing permit.
The Administrator ensures that smoking, candles, space heaters, cooking equipment and oxygen use follow SAF-08, HCS-03 and the fire authority's directions, and that oxygen is stored and used safely.
The Administrator trains new staff on fire procedures, alarm and extinguisher use, and evacuation techniques before they work alone, and repeats training at least annually (STF-03).
The Administrator reviews the fire plan and drill record at least annually and after any fire, failed drill or change in building or resident needs (GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Obtain and keep fire clearances, maintain equipment, assign fire duties, conduct drills, make reports and correct deficiencies.
Carry out fire responsibilities when the Administrator is absent.
Keep exits clear, know alarm and extinguisher use, take part in drills and evacuate residents.
Inspect the facility and issue fire clearances.

documentation: Fire clearances, including the separate clearance for nonambulatory or bedridden residents
Fire safety plan and posted exit diagrams
Fire drill records for each shift
Equipment inspection and testing records
Reports to fire authority and licensing after any fire or explosion
Staff fire training records
Corrective action logs

policies.title: Infection Prevention and Control Plan
policies.applies_to: All staff, volunteers and contracted providers at [AGENCY NAME] (California RCFE)
federal: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 (bloodborne pathogens; employees with occupational exposure)
policies.purpose: To prevent and control infections among residents, staff and visitors through a written plan, a trained Infection Control Lead, staff training and prompt outbreak response and reporting.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains a written infection control plan on form LIC 9282 and names an Infection Control Lead who has been trained by a qualified professional, as 22 CCR §87470 requires. The plan sets initial and ongoing staff training and is reviewed at least annually, after an outbreak declaration and at the licensing agency's request. Staff training includes infection control (22 CCR §87411), and the licensee maintains infection control practices (22 CCR §87465). Residents with serious infections that are prohibited conditions, such as staph infections, are not retained unless the regulations allow (ADM-04). Outbreaks are reported to licensing and the local health officer within 24 hours. Staff with occupational exposure to blood or body fluids are protected under the federal OSHA bloodborne pathogens standard.

definitions.definition: The designated staff member trained by a qualified professional who oversees the infection control plan, training and response.
An occurrence of illness or infection among residents or staff in excess of what is expected, or that a local health officer declares an outbreak.
Practices applied to all residents, including hand hygiene, glove and PPE use, safe handling of sharps and waste, and cleaning and disinfection.
Reasonably anticipated contact with blood or other potentially infectious materials during an employee's duties.

procedures: The Administrator completes the written infection control plan on LIC 9282 before licensure and keeps it on site.

The Administrator names the Infection Control Lead in writing [INFECTION CONTROL LEAD] and arranges for that person's training from a qualified professional. The training certificate is placed in the personnel file. A trained alternate is named for absences.

The plan sets standard precautions: hand hygiene before and after resident contact, glove and PPE use, respiratory etiquette, safe food handling, linen and laundry handling, cleaning and disinfection of high-touch surfaces and shared equipment, and safe disposal of waste.

The Administrator trains every new employee in infection control before the employee works alone and gives refresher training at least annually and when the plan changes. The date, topics, trainer and signatures are recorded in personnel records.

The Administrator determines whether any employee has occupational exposure to blood or body fluids. If so, the facility develops a written exposure control plan under OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 that covers training, protective equipment, hepatitis B vaccine offer, sharps handling and post-exposure follow-up.

Staff wash hands, use gloves and clean up spills with a facility-approved disinfectant. Used sharps, if any, are placed immediately in a puncture-resistant container. Soiled linen is bagged at the point of use and washed separately according to the plan.

Staff who are ill with symptoms of contagious illness, such as fever, vomiting, diarrhea or a rash, report to the Administrator before the shift and are excluded from resident care as the plan sets out. TB screening and health screening are handled under STF-04.
Staff observe residents daily for signs of infection and report changes to the Administrator. Changes of condition are handled under HCS-05, and the physician is notified.
The Administrator does not admit or retain a resident with a prohibited infectious condition (ADM-01, ADM-04) and arranges transfer or medical care if a resident develops one.

If two or more residents or staff develop similar illness, the Administrator notifies the local health officer, begins isolation and cohorting as advised, increases cleaning, and tracks cases on a line list.
The Administrator reports any outbreak to the licensing agency and the local health officer within 24 hours by phone or fax, then follows with written reports as required (SAF-02, REC-02).
The Administrator notifies residents' responsible persons and physicians of an outbreak and tells visitors about any visiting restrictions, while protecting resident rights (SAF-08, RR-01).
The Administrator keeps necessary supplies on hand, including soap, hand sanitizer, gloves, masks, disinfectants, thermometers and first aid supplies.

The Administrator reviews and updates the plan at least annually, after any outbreak declaration and whenever licensing asks, and records the review date and revisions. The review is part of quality assurance (GOV-05).
Immunization and infection information for residents is kept in the resident record as the plan and resident privacy rules permit (RR-07, REC-01).

responsibilities.duty: Maintain the plan, name and support the Infection Control Lead, ensure training, report outbreaks and review the plan.
Oversee practices, monitor compliance, coordinate response to illness and outbreaks, and advise staff.
Follow standard precautions, report symptoms, and complete training.
Receive outbreak reports and give guidance.

documentation: Written infection control plan (LIC 9282) and review log
Infection Control Lead designation and training certificate
Staff infection control training records
Exposure control plan, if applicable
Outbreak line lists and reports to licensing and the local health officer
Cleaning logs
Staff illness reporting records

policies.title: Smoking, Visitors, Pets and Firearms
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all staff, residents, visitors and volunteers at [AGENCY NAME] (California RCFE)
policies.purpose: To set fair, written rules on smoking, visitors, pets and firearms that keep residents safe and respect their personal rights, and to make sure the rules are disclosed in the admission agreement.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] has written house policies on visiting, firearms, smoking and pets. The visiting policy follows state law and is included in each admission agreement (22 CCR §87507), and residents have the right to be told about it (22 CCR §87468.1). Visitors, including ombudsmen and advocacy representatives, may visit residents privately during reasonable hours without prior notice, as long as other residents' rights are not infringed (22 CCR §87468.1). The firearms policy, including whether residents may keep firearms and how they must be stored, is stated in the admission agreement. Facility house policies are reasonable and do not violate residents' rights (22 CCR §87507). Smoking and pets are governed by local ordinance, the fire authority's directions and the Plan of Operation, and any rule on them is disclosed before admission.

definitions.definition: Any person who visits a resident, including family, friends, clergy, ombudsmen and advocates.
Visiting hours that are set in the visiting policy and do not unreasonably limit access, and that are never used to bar ombudsmen or advocacy representatives.
Any gun, ammunition or weapon covered by the facility's firearms policy.
A written facility rule disclosed in the admission agreement that governs conduct in the facility.

procedures: The Administrator writes the visiting policy to follow state law, states visiting hours, and includes it in the admission agreement. The policy provides that residents may receive visitors privately and that ombudsmen and advocates may visit without notice during reasonable hours.
The Administrator reviews the visiting policy with each applicant and representative before the agreement is signed, and gives a copy as part of the signed admission agreement (RR-04).
Staff greet visitors courteously, ask them to sign in and out as the facility's policy provides, and escort them to the resident or allow privacy as the resident chooses.
Staff never deny entry to an ombudsman, licensing representative or advocacy representative. They notify the Administrator but do not delay or require prior notice for the visit (RR-03).
A resident may limit or refuse any visitor. Staff honor that choice and document it.

The Administrator may limit a visit only when it would infringe on other residents' rights, such as privacy or safety, or when a lawful reason exists such as an outbreak or a safety threat. Any limit is applied no more than needed, explained to the resident and visitor, and documented.

The Administrator states in the admission agreement the facility's firearms policy, including whether residents may keep firearms. If firearms are permitted, they are stored as state law requires and in a way that protects other residents and staff. If not permitted, the agreement says so and the Administrator tells the resident before admission.

If staff learn that a firearm is in the facility, they notify the Administrator at once. The Administrator secures it in accordance with the policy, calls law enforcement if there is a threat, and documents the response.

The Administrator sets any smoking rules in the Plan of Operation in line with local ordinance and fire authority guidance, including whether smoking is allowed, where, and under what supervision. The rules are disclosed in the admission agreement. Oxygen and smoking are never combined (SAF-06).

The Administrator sets any rules on resident-owned pets or visiting animals in the Plan of Operation in line with local ordinance and the owner's approval, covering vaccination, care responsibility, allergies and the safety of other residents. The rules are disclosed before admission.
The Administrator applies house policies equally to all residents and does not use them to discriminate or to restrict rights (RR-01, RR-08).
The Administrator reviews house policies at least annually with the Plan of Operation (GOV-04) and when a resident, family or the Resident Council raises a concern (RR-09).

responsibilities.duty: Write and disclose house policies, honor visitor rights, secure any firearm, and review the policies annually.
Apply the policies in the Administrator's absence.
Welcome visitors, allow privacy, never block ombudsman or advocate access, and report firearm or safety concerns.
Follow house policies and respect other residents' rights.

documentation: Visiting, firearms, smoking and pet policies in the Plan of Operation
Signed admission agreement showing disclosure
Visitor sign-in log
Records of any visit limits and reasons
Firearm incident reports and law enforcement contacts
Annual policy review notes

policies.title: Food Service, Sample Menu and Therapeutic Diets
policies.applies_to: Administrator, food service and direct care staff, and residents of [AGENCY NAME] (California RCFE)
policies.purpose: To provide nutritious, safe, appealing meals that meet residents' needs and preferences, including physician-ordered therapeutic diets, and to meet the sample menu and staff knowledge requirements for licensure.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides food service as described in its Plan of Operation. A sample menu is submitted with the license application (LIC 281, item B10). Staff who plan or prepare food have knowledge of good nutrition, food preparation and storage, and menu planning (22 CCR §87411). Therapeutic diets are provided only on a physician's order and are included in the resident's service plan. Residents are not denied food as punishment, and if ALW participation applies, residents have access to food as federal HCBS rules require. Food service is carried out in accordance with the food service regulations of Title 22 and local health requirements, which the Administrator reviews before opening and whenever they change.

definitions.definition: A written menu submitted with the license application (LIC 281 B10) that shows the meals and snacks the facility will offer.
A special diet ordered by a physician for a medical condition, such as low sodium, diabetic, renal or texture-modified.
A diet in which food or liquid consistency is changed, such as chopped, pureed or thickened, for chewing or swallowing difficulty.
A resident's documented adverse reaction to a food that must be avoided.

procedures: Before applying, the Administrator prepares a sample menu showing meals and snacks and submits it with the application as LIC 281 requires (item B10). The menu reflects the Plan of Operation food service description.

The Administrator confirms that each person who plans menus or prepares food has the knowledge required by 22 CCR §87411 on good nutrition, food preparation and storage, and menu planning. Training and experience are recorded in the personnel file (STF-03, STF-05).

The Administrator or designee prepares menus in advance, varies them to meet residents' nutritional needs, preferences, and cultural and religious practices, and posts the current menu where residents can see it.

During the admission appraisal and each reassessment, staff record each resident's dietary needs, allergies, food preferences, swallowing or chewing problems, weight concerns and any physician-ordered diet (ADM-01, ADM-02).

A therapeutic diet is started only on a written physician's order. The Administrator places the order in the resident's record, adds the diet to the service plan (ADM-03), and tells the cook and all staff who serve food.
Staff keep a current list of each resident's diet orders and allergies in the kitchen, and check it before every meal service to make sure each resident gets the correct food and texture.

If a resident cannot be safely fed by the facility, such as a need for tube feeding or other care beyond what the license allows, the Administrator follows ADM-04 and ADM-05 to decide whether the resident can be served.

Staff store, prepare, hold and serve food in a sanitary way. This includes handwashing, clean surfaces and equipment, separating raw and ready-to-eat foods, labeling and dating stored food, keeping perishable food at safe temperatures, and following local health department requirements (SAF-07, DL-03).

Staff offer meals and snacks at times set in the Plan of Operation, give help with eating when the service plan calls for it, and allow residents enough time to eat. Staff do not rush or force a resident to eat.
Staff keep fresh drinking water available to residents at all times and offer fluids regularly, especially to residents at risk of dehydration.

Residents are not denied food or drink as punishment. If a restriction is medically ordered, it is documented. If ALW participation applies, any limit on a resident's access to food is documented in the service plan as a modification with the assessed need and the resident's consent (GOV-08, SAF-04).
Staff report significant changes in appetite, weight, swallowing or hydration to the Administrator, who notifies the physician and the responsible person (HCS-05).

When a substitution is needed, staff replace it with food of comparable nutrition and note the substitution on the menu record. Staff accommodate resident choice and Resident Council suggestions where possible (RR-09).
The Administrator keeps menus as served, diet orders and kitchen cleaning records, and reviews the menu and food service quarterly with resident feedback and quality assurance (GOV-05).
The Administrator checks the food service requirements in Title 22 and local health rules before opening and annually, and updates this policy if a requirement changes.

responsibilities.duty: Prepare the sample menu, ensure staff have the required knowledge, obtain diet orders, oversee food safety and review food service.
Prepare and serve food safely according to the menu and diet orders, and follow the allergy list.
Serve and assist with meals as per the service plan and report changes in eating or weight.
Order and review therapeutic diets.
Share dietary needs and preferences and give feedback on meals.

documentation: Sample menu (LIC 281 B10) and posted menus
Menus as served with substitutions
Physician diet orders
Resident diet and allergy list
Service plan entries on nutrition
Staff training and experience records on nutrition and food safety
Kitchen cleaning and food storage logs
Quarterly food service review notes

policies.title: Activities and Social Programming
policies.applies_to: All residents, administrator, direct care staff, activity staff and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure each resident has access to planned, meaningful activities that support recreation, companionship, independence and dignity. The program must be run by staff who understand residents' psychosocial needs, and it must fit the needs of residents with dementia.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides a planned activity program that offers residents regular opportunities for recreation, social contact, and independence. Participation is always voluntary. Staff who care for residents are trained in residents' psychosocial needs, including recreation, companionship and independence (22 CCR §87411(c)(3)(E)). Residents may attend religious services of their choice, and no resident is required to attend or barred from attending. Activities are adapted to each resident's abilities, interests, language and culture, as identified in the resident's appraisal and Individualized Service Plan. For residents with dementia, activities are matched to appraised needs. In homes with fewer than 16 beds, awake night staff are provided when a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision, based on appraisal, reappraisal or observation (22 CCR §87705). If [AGENCY NAME] advertises or holds itself out as providing a dementia program, the activity component of that program is written into the plan of operation and carried out as described. Volunteers who help with activities are supervised and are not counted toward required staffing (22 CCR §87411).

definitions.definition: A scheduled or standing recreational, social, creative, physical, cognitive or spiritual offering that staff organize and post for residents.
A resident's needs for recreation, companionship, independence, meaningful roles and emotional well-being.
A resident's right to choose, accept or decline any activity, including religious services, without penalty or pressure.

procedures: At admission, the administrator or designee records each resident's interests, past routines, hobbies, faith practices, language, social preferences and abilities in the pre-admission appraisal (see ADM-01) and carries them into the Individualized Service Plan (see ADM-03).
The administrator designates a staff member as activity coordinator and lists this duty in the staff's job description. If no one is designated, the administrator holds this responsibility.

The activity coordinator writes a monthly activity calendar. It includes at least one offering each day and a mix of physical, social, cognitive, creative and spiritual options, including options for residents who prefer quiet or in-room activities.

The calendar is posted in a common area at resident eye level by the 25th of the prior month. A copy is available on request to residents and their representatives. Changes are marked on the posted calendar the same day.
Staff invite residents to activities and offer reminders or escorts as needed. A resident's decision to decline is respected and noted when it forms a pattern.
The coordinator arranges access to religious services of each resident's choice, either on site or in the community, and makes sure residents are not required to take part in any religious activity.

Staff provide one-to-one or small-group engagement for residents who cannot or will not join group activities, such as bedbound residents or those with sensory loss, and record it on the activity log.

For residents with dementia, the coordinator adapts activities to the resident's cognitive level, uses familiar routines and avoids over-stimulation. Staff do not use activities as a means of restraint or behavioral control (see HCS-06 and SAF-04).
Direct care staff complete the required training on psychosocial needs, including recreation, companionship and independence, as part of orientation and annual training (see STF-03).
Staff record each activity offered and resident participation on the daily activity log before the end of the shift. They note any decline in participation, mood or interest.

If a resident's participation drops sharply or mood changes, the staff member reports it to the administrator the same day. The administrator decides whether a reassessment or notice to the resident's representative or physician is needed (see ADM-02 and HCS-05).
Volunteers and outside entertainers are screened as required (see STF-02), supervised by a staff member at all times, and not counted in staffing (see STF-01).

If [AGENCY NAME] advertises a dementia program, the administrator makes sure the plan of operation describes the program's activities. The administrator reviews the written program at least annually (see HCS-06 and GOV-04).

The administrator reviews the activity calendar and logs at least quarterly with residents and the Resident Council to gather requests for new activities (see RR-09 and GOV-05), and records changes made.

responsibilities.duty: Assign an activity coordinator, make sure the program is resourced and consistent with the plan of operation, and review logs and resident feedback at least quarterly.
Develop, post and adapt the monthly calendar, document participation, and make sure religious and individual preferences are honored.
Encourage and assist residents' participation, respect declination, and report changes in mood or engagement.
Assist only under staff supervision and within the roles set by the administrator.

documentation: Monthly activity calendars
Daily activity and participation logs
Resident interest and preference information in the appraisal and Individualized Service Plan
Resident Council minutes and feedback regarding activities
Staff training records on psychosocial needs
Written dementia program description, if advertised

policies.title: Housekeeping, Laundry, Maintenance and Physical Plant
policies.applies_to: Administrator, maintenance and housekeeping staff, direct care staff and the entire licensed premises of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To keep the facility clean, safe, comfortable and in good repair, and to meet California requirements for heating, hot water, bedroom occupancy, bathing and toileting fixtures, water supply testing and resident storage space.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] maintains the building, grounds, furniture and equipment in a clean, safe, sanitary and good working condition. Residents are entitled to safe, healthful and comfortable accommodations, and to individual storage space for personal belongings (22 CCR §87468.1). Resident rooms are heated to at least 68°F, and hot water at fixtures accessible to residents is kept between 105°F and 120°F (22 CCR §87303). No bedroom houses more than 2 residents. The home provides at least one toilet and washbasin for every 6 persons and at least one tub or shower for every 10 persons, counting live-in staff and family members who use the same fixtures (22 CCR §87307). If the facility has a private water supply, it is tested annually when licensed capacity is 7 to 15. For capacity of 6 or fewer, testing is done when evidence shows a need. Staff who do housekeeping and sanitation tasks are trained in housekeeping and sanitation (22 CCR §87411(d)(2)).

definitions.definition: A well or other water source not provided by a public water system.
Scheduled inspection, servicing and repair that keeps the building, systems and equipment working and prevents hazards.
Space such as a closet, dresser or locked drawer assigned to a resident for personal belongings.

procedures: The administrator keeps a written housekeeping, laundry and maintenance schedule that assigns daily, weekly, monthly and annual tasks to named positions, and reviews it at least annually.

Housekeeping staff clean resident rooms, bathrooms and common areas on the posted schedule, and clean immediately after spills, soiling or incontinence episodes, using products and methods described in the infection control plan (see SAF-07).
Cleaning chemicals are stored in a locked area away from food and medications. Safety data sheets are kept available to staff.

Laundry is handled by trained staff. Soiled linen is bagged at the point of use and kept separate from clean linen. Linens are washed with a detergent and temperature appropriate for the item, and clean items are stored covered in a clean location.
Resident clothing is laundered on request and labeled to prevent loss. Losses and damage are handled under RR-05.

Before admission and at least monthly, the maintenance designee checks every resident room and bathroom for working heat, plumbing, lights, call or alert devices if installed, door locks and window security, and records the results on the maintenance log.

Staff measure the temperature in resident rooms each month during the heating season with a thermometer. If the temperature is below 68°F, they notify the administrator the same day. The administrator provides safe supplemental heat or relocates residents until the problem is corrected.

Staff test hot water at accessible fixtures at least monthly, and after any water heater service, with a thermometer. They record the readings and fix any reading outside 105°F to 120°F immediately. Water heater settings are changed by the maintenance designee, and the administrator is notified.

Before assigning rooms, the administrator verifies that no bedroom exceeds 2 residents and that the facility meets the ratio of one toilet and washbasin per 6 persons and one tub or shower per 10 persons, counting live-in staff and family. The count is recalculated whenever occupancy or live-in household members change.

The administrator assigns each resident individual storage space for clothing and belongings and allows residents to bring and arrange personal items in their rooms, subject to safety. Room and restroom assignments are made without discrimination (see RR-08).

If [AGENCY NAME] uses a private water supply, the administrator arranges testing by a qualified laboratory every year when licensed capacity is 7 to 15. For capacity of 6 or fewer, testing is arranged when evidence shows a need. Results are kept on file. A failed test is corrected, and the administrator takes protective action for residents, such as providing bottled water, until a passing result.

Staff report any hazard, such as a broken handrail, uneven flooring, a leak, a pest sighting or an inoperable appliance, to the maintenance designee the same shift. The designee posts a hazard notice, takes temporary protective action, and records the date of the repair.
The administrator schedules pest control and servicing of heating and cooling, fire protection and kitchen equipment as needed, and keeps service records.
Housekeeping and laundry staff receive training on housekeeping and sanitation during orientation and annually (see STF-03). The training is documented in the personnel record.

The administrator inspects the home at least quarterly with a written checklist covering cleanliness, repairs, temperatures, bedroom and fixture counts, and storage, and reports findings in the internal compliance review (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Make sure the premises meet occupancy, fixture, heat, hot water and water testing requirements. Approve repairs and review inspections.
Carry out preventive maintenance, temperature checks and repairs, and keep the maintenance log.
Perform cleaning and laundry tasks on schedule according to infection control procedures, and report hazards.
Report maintenance and safety concerns and help residents keep personal storage orderly.

documentation: Housekeeping and laundry schedules
Monthly maintenance, room temperature and hot water logs
Bedroom occupancy and fixture-ratio worksheet
Water test results (where applicable)
Repair and service records, including pest control
Quarterly premises inspection checklists
Staff training records on housekeeping and sanitation

policies.title: Transportation
policies.applies_to: Administrator, drivers, direct care staff and residents of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure residents can get to needed medical and dental care and other appointments, and that transportation arrangements are described in the plan of operation and the evacuation plan.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] provides transportation to medical and dental care directly or through arrangement, as part of its incidental medical and dental care plan. Transportation to medical or dental care may be limited to the nearest available facility that meets the resident's need (22 CCR §87465(a)(2)). The way [AGENCY NAME] provides or arranges transportation is described in the plan of operation (22 CCR §87208) and is also reflected in the facility's emergency and evacuation plan. Emergency transport is by 9-1-1. The facility does not delay calling 9-1-1 to transport a resident by facility vehicle in a life-threatening situation. The driver, vehicle and insurance standards in this policy are [AGENCY NAME] practices and are not quoted from a state transportation rule.

definitions.definition: The closest medical or dental provider that can meet the resident's need and has an appointment or service available.
Transportation set up by the facility with a third party, such as a family member, public paratransit, a contracted van, or a medical transport company.

procedures: The administrator documents in the plan of operation whether [AGENCY NAME] provides transportation directly, arranges it, or both. The plan lists the types of trips covered, any fees disclosed in the admission agreement, and how residents request rides (see RR-04 and GOV-04).
At admission, staff explain the transportation arrangements to the resident and representative, including medical and dental appointment transport and what is not provided.

Residents or their representatives tell staff about appointments as early as possible. Staff enter the appointment on a shared transportation calendar, including the date, time, destination, mobility needs and who is accompanying the resident.

When a resident needs medical or dental care, staff arrange transportation to the nearest available provider that can meet the need. If a resident or representative prefers another provider, staff explain that the facility's responsibility is limited to the nearest available one. Any extra transportation or escort is arranged as described in the admission agreement.

If the facility provides transportation, the administrator confirms in advance that each driver holds a valid California driver's license for the vehicle class, has had clearance under STF-02 where the driver works in the facility, and is physically able to assist residents.
Before each trip, the driver checks the vehicle's tires, lights, brakes, mirrors, seat belts and any wheelchair lift or securement device, and records the pre-trip check.
Staff make sure each resident is seated with a seat belt fastened, wheelchairs are secured by the vehicle's securement system, and walkers and oxygen are stored safely.

The driver or escort carries the resident's face sheet, emergency contacts, medication list, advance directive or POLST if applicable (see RR-06), and the facility phone number. Information is shared only as needed for care (see RR-07).
Staff accompany residents who need supervision, such as those with dementia or elopement risk, and never leave a resident unattended in a vehicle (see SAF-03).
The driver reports an accident, injury or breakdown to the administrator immediately. The administrator handles the incident under SAF-02 and any required notice under REC-02.
If a resident has an emergency during transport, the driver stops safely and calls 9-1-1. The driver then notifies the administrator and the resident's representative.

Staff record each trip on the transportation log with date, resident, destination, driver, departure and return times, and any problems. Staff note the outcome of medical appointments in the resident record and notify the physician or representative of any changes (see HCS-05).

The administrator confirms that the facility's liability and auto insurance cover transportation (see GOV-07) and reviews the evacuation plan at least annually to make sure transportation arrangements for evacuation are current (see SAF-05).
The administrator reviews transportation logs and complaints at least quarterly and corrects problems such as missed appointments or delays (see RR-02 and GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Define and document transportation arrangements in the plan of operation, verify driver and vehicle standards and insurance, and review the logs.
Hold a valid license, do pre-trip checks, transport residents safely and complete the trip log.
Schedule appointments, prepare residents and paperwork, escort residents when needed and follow up on results.
Give notice of appointments and share any preference for a provider.

documentation: Plan of operation section on transportation
Transportation calendar and trip logs
Vehicle pre-trip check records and maintenance records
Driver license and clearance records
Insurance documentation covering transportation
Incident reports for transport events

policies.title: Staffing Levels, Night Supervision and Supervision
policies.applies_to: Administrator, all employees, volunteers and live-in staff of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure [AGENCY NAME] has enough competent staff at all times to meet residents' needs, including required overnight supervision, and that residents and volunteers are never used to meet staffing requirements.
policies.policy: California sets no fixed numeric day-shift staff-to-resident ratio for RCFEs. [AGENCY NAME] must always have personnel sufficient in numbers and competent to provide the services residents need, and CDSS Community Care Licensing may require more staff when documentation shows a need (22 CCR §87411(a)). Anyone who supervises staff or residents must be at least 18 years old (22 CCR §87411(b)). Residents may not be used as substitutes for required staff, and volunteers must be supervised and are not counted in the staffing plan (22 CCR §87411(i),(j)). Night supervision from 10 p.m. to 6 a.m. follows 22 CCR §87415. For fewer than 16 residents, a qualified person must be on call on the premises overnight. For 16 to 100 residents, one employee must be awake and on duty, with one more employee on call within 10 minutes. In homes with fewer than 16 beds, at least one night staff person must be awake and on duty when a resident with dementia needs awake night supervision, as shown by appraisal, reappraisal or observation (22 CCR §87705). Night staff must know the emergency plan and be trained in first aid (22 CCR §87415).

definitions.definition: At least one qualified staff person who is awake, alert and on duty on the premises during night hours (10 p.m. to 6 a.m.).
A qualified person who is present in the facility overnight and available to respond promptly when needed.
Employees who assist residents with activities of daily living or provide supervision.
The Personnel Report form that lists staff and the hours and shifts they cover.

procedures: The administrator prepares a written staffing plan before opening and updates it whenever residents' needs, census or licensed capacity change. The plan states the number and type of staff on each shift (day, evening, night) and is based on residents' appraisals and Individualized Service Plans (see ADM-02 and ADM-03).

The administrator reviews staffing at least weekly and whenever a new resident is admitted, a resident's condition changes or hospice starts. Additional staff are scheduled before the need is unmet. The review is recorded.
The administrator completes the LIC 500 Personnel Report to show who covers each shift, and updates it when staff or schedules change. The LIC 500 is kept available for CDSS review.

Staff schedules are posted in advance and show the name, job title and hours of every person on duty. Actual hours worked are recorded on time records (see STF-07). If a person is absent, the administrator or designee finds a qualified replacement before the shift starts.
Only persons age 18 or older are assigned to supervise staff or residents. The administrator checks age on hire and records it in the personnel file (see STF-05).

No resident performs required staff duties or is counted toward staffing. Volunteers work only under staff supervision, perform non-care duties assigned by the administrator, and are never counted in the staffing plan.
No staff member provides care until they have a criminal record clearance or exemption and have completed the minimum training required before working alone (see STF-02 and STF-03).

Fewer than 16 residents: the administrator assigns a qualified person to be on call on the premises every night, in a place from which they can hear and respond to residents. The person's name is on the night schedule.

Fewer than 16 residents with dementia: at each appraisal, reappraisal and when staff observe a change, the administrator decides whether any resident with dementia needs awake night supervision (for example, wandering, night waking, confusion, or exit-seeking). If so, the administrator assigns at least one night staff person who stays awake and on duty all night, and documents the decision in the resident record (see HCS-06).

16 to 100 residents: the administrator schedules one employee awake and on duty overnight and a second employee on call who can reach the facility within 10 minutes. The name and phone number of the on-call employee are posted on the night schedule and at the staff station.

The administrator prepares an awake night duty statement describing awake and on-call responsibilities, such as rounds, response to call systems, medication-related concerns, emergency response and who to call. Each night staff member signs it at hire and after any change, and it is kept in the personnel file.

Before working a night shift, each night staff member shows proof of current first aid training and is oriented to the emergency plan, fire evacuation, disaster procedures and 9-1-1 and notification steps (see SAF-05 and SAF-06). Orientation is documented.

Night staff stay awake while on duty if awake supervision is required, make and record rounds at intervals set by the administrator, and notify the administrator or on-call person of incidents (see SAF-02).
The administrator supervises staff through regular observation, at least quarterly performance feedback, and prompt correction of problems. Supervision notes are kept in personnel files.

When a resident's need, a complaint or a CDSS finding indicates staffing is not sufficient, the administrator adds staff immediately, documents the change, and reviews the effect at the next internal compliance review (see GOV-05).
The administrator reviews the staffing plan, night schedules and LIC 500 at least annually and before any increase in licensed capacity.

responsibilities.duty: Set and adjust staffing, assign night coverage, complete the LIC 500, and keep night duty statements and records.
Remain awake or on call as assigned, carry out emergency procedures, keep first aid training current, and sign the night duty statement.
Report changes in resident needs that may require added staffing.
Provide the resources necessary to maintain staffing at all times.

documentation: Written staffing plan
LIC 500 Personnel Report
Posted staff schedules and time records
Awake night duty statements signed by night staff
Night rounds records
Documentation of dementia-related awake supervision decisions
First aid and emergency plan orientation records

policies.title: Criminal Record Clearance and Background Checks
policies.applies_to: Licensee, administrator, adult household members, employees and volunteers of [AGENCY NAME] who are subject to criminal record review
policies.purpose: To make sure everyone who must have a criminal record review has a California clearance or exemption before working at, or being present in, the facility, in order to protect residents.
policies.policy: No one subject to criminal record review may be employed by, volunteer at or be present in [AGENCY NAME] until they have a California criminal record clearance or exemption, or have requested a transfer of a clearance or exemption (22 CCR §87411(g)). DOJ and FBI Live Scan fingerprint clearance, or an exemption, is required for the applicant, administrator and adult household members before licensure, and for staff before they work or are present (22 CCR §87355). A person who does not have a clearance, exemption or accepted transfer may not work, volunteer, or have contact with residents. Each person completes a criminal record statement (LIC 508) as part of personnel documentation. [AGENCY NAME] does not rely on any registry check that has not been verified as an RCFE requirement and does not treat any such check as a substitute for fingerprint clearance.

definitions.definition: Electronic fingerprinting used to submit a person's fingerprints to the California Department of Justice and the FBI.
CDSS confirmation that a person has no disqualifying criminal history or that the history is acceptable.
A CDSS decision allowing a person with a criminal conviction to be present or work in the facility.
A request to move an existing clearance or exemption to a new facility.
The criminal record statement completed by the person subject to review.

procedures: Before offering a position or accepting a volunteer, the administrator determines whether the person is subject to criminal record review. The administrator treats all employees, volunteers with resident contact or regular presence, and adult household members as subject to review unless CDSS confirms otherwise.
Before the person's first day, the administrator gives the person the LIC 508 criminal record statement and explains the clearance process. The person completes and signs the form.

The administrator arranges for fingerprinting through Live Scan using the facility's CDSS Community Care Licensing ID, or checks whether a clearance or exemption already exists that can be transferred to the facility.

If the person has an existing clearance or exemption, the administrator requests a transfer to [AGENCY NAME] through the process CDSS provides, and records the date of the request. The person may begin work or be present only as allowed under 22 CCR §87411(g).
The administrator keeps a clearance tracking log listing each person, role, Live Scan date, clearance or exemption status, and transfer request date.

No person works, volunteers or stays at the facility unsupervised, or has contact with residents, until the administrator confirms clearance, exemption, or an accepted transfer as required by regulation. The administrator updates the schedule so that the person is not counted in staffing until cleared (see STF-01).
For the licensee, administrator and adult household members, the administrator confirms DOJ and FBI clearance or exemption before licensure and keeps the proof on file.

The administrator reviews the written clearance notice from CDSS for each person. If CDSS denies clearance or requires an exemption, the person is removed from duty and facility presence immediately until the matter is resolved.
If the person has a criminal conviction, the administrator follows the exemption process CDSS directs and does not allow the person to work or be present unless an exemption is granted.

When a new adult moves into the household, a new live-in staff member is added, or a person's role changes, the administrator starts the criminal record process before the person arrives or starts duties.
The administrator keeps the LIC 508 and clearance or exemption documents in the personnel file and makes them available to CDSS on request (see STF-05).

Staff must tell the administrator promptly if they are arrested for, or convicted of, any crime. The administrator then follows CDSS direction and does not assume the clearance remains valid without checking.
The administrator audits the clearance log at least quarterly and before every inspection to make sure there are no gaps, and documents the audit in the internal compliance review (see GOV-05).
Employment decisions based on background results are made without discrimination and follow applicable state and federal law.

responsibilities.duty: Determine who is subject to review, start Live Scan or transfer, keep the tracking log, and keep unclear persons off duty.
Make sure the licensee and all adult household members are cleared before licensure and that the administrator follows this policy.
Complete the LIC 508 and fingerprinting honestly and report any arrest or conviction promptly.

documentation: LIC 508 criminal record statements
Live Scan submission records
CDSS clearance, exemption and transfer notices
Clearance tracking log
Quarterly audit of the clearance log
Removal-from-duty notes, if any

policies.title: Hiring, Orientation and Ongoing Training
policies.applies_to: Administrator, direct care staff, other employees and trainers of [AGENCY NAME]
policies.purpose: To make sure every staff member is competent, trained before working alone, and kept current on required topics, including first aid, dementia, postural supports, restricted health conditions, hospice and medication assistance.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] hires only personnel who are cleared (see STF-02) and trains them to meet California requirements before they work alone and continuously after. Direct care staff complete 40 hours of initial training: 20 hours before working alone, including 6 hours of dementia and 4 hours on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice, and the remaining 20 hours within 4 weeks of hire, including 6 more hours of dementia (HSC §§1569.625, 1569.626). Direct care staff then complete 20 hours annually, including 8 hours of dementia and 4 hours on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice. Staff who provide care also hold first aid training from a qualified provider such as the American Red Cross (22 CCR §87411(c)(1)). Required training topics include the aging process, personal care and infection control, residents' rights, medication policies, psychosocial needs and signs of dementia (22 CCR §87411(c)(3)). Staff who assist with self-administered medication complete the medication assistance training under HSC §1569.69 (see HCS-02). Training is documented in the personnel file (22 CCR §87411(c)(6)).

definitions.definition: The 40 hours of training that direct care staff complete after hire, 20 hours before working alone and 20 hours within 4 weeks.
The 20 hours of training direct care staff complete each year.
A trainer who has a degree plus 2 years of experience, a health care license, or 2 years' experience as an RCFE administrator within the past 8 years.
Training delivered at the facility by a qualified trainer while the staff member performs tasks under supervision.

procedures: The administrator keeps a written job description for each position that lists duties, required qualifications, training and who the position reports to. Before hire, the administrator confirms the applicant is at least 18 if the position supervises residents or staff (see STF-01).

Before the start date, the administrator confirms criminal record clearance, exemption or accepted transfer (see STF-02) and health screening requirements (see STF-04). The new hire does not work until these are done.

On or before day one, the administrator gives the new hire an orientation covering the facility's policies, residents' rights, abuse reporting, emergency and evacuation procedures, infection control and the job description. The new hire signs an orientation acknowledgment.

Direct care staff complete 20 hours of training before working alone. The 20 hours include 6 hours of dementia and 4 hours on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice. Until then, the new hire works only with a trained, qualified staff member, and is not counted toward staffing minimums while unsupervised hours are not allowed.

Direct care staff complete the other 20 hours of initial training within 4 weeks of hire, including 6 more hours of dementia, for a total of 12 hours of dementia training at initial training (HSC §1569.626). The administrator sets a due date on the training tracker and follows up weekly.

Direct care staff must have first aid training from a qualified provider such as the American Red Cross. The administrator confirms current first aid training at hire and again before expiration and keeps a copy of the card or certificate.

Training covers the topics in 22 CCR §87411(c)(3): the aging process, personal care and infection control, residents' rights, medication policies, psychosocial needs and signs of dementia, plus other topics needed for the person's tasks.

The administrator confirms that each trainer is qualified under 22 CCR §87411(c)(4): a degree plus 2 years' experience, a health care license, or 2 years as an RCFE administrator within the past 8 years. The trainer's qualifications are kept on file.

For on-the-job training, the trainer gives a signed statement of the content covered and the hours, and the administrator files it in the personnel record. For classroom or outside training, staff keep the certificate and provide a copy.

Staff who will assist with self-administered medications complete HSC §1569.69 training before assisting: for homes with 15 or fewer residents, 10 hours initial (6 hours hands-on before assisting and 4 hours within 2 weeks) plus an exam. For homes with 16 or more residents, 24 hours initial (16 hours hands-on before assisting and 8 hours within 4 weeks) plus an exam. Medication assistance training is 8 hours annually after that. No one assists with medication until they pass the exam and the administrator authorizes them in writing (see HCS-02).

Facilities with 16 or more residents may satisfy the topic training under 22 CCR §87411(d) through a planned on-the-job training program (22 CCR §87411(e)). If [AGENCY NAME] has 16 or more residents, the administrator documents the program, its trainers and its content in the plan of operation (see GOV-04).

After the initial period, direct care staff complete 20 hours annually, including 8 hours of dementia and 4 hours on postural supports, restricted health conditions and hospice. The administrator schedules training in the first half of the year to allow time for make-up sessions.

The administrator keeps a training tracker with each person's hire date, hours complete by category, first aid expiration, medication training and exam dates, and due dates. The administrator reviews it monthly and takes anyone who is behind off unsupervised care duties until they catch up.

The administrator completes the administrator certification requirements of HSC §1569.616 (80-hour program and state exam within 60 days, and 40 hours of continuing education every 2 years including 8 hours on dementia) and keeps the certificate current (see GOV-02).
Staff sign in on a training roster for every in-service session. The roster shows the date, topic, hours, trainer and attendees. Records are filed in each personnel record (see STF-05).
The administrator evaluates the training program yearly, asks staff for needs, and adds training after incidents, new resident conditions or regulatory changes (see GOV-05).

responsibilities.duty: Verify qualifications, schedule and track all training, make sure staff do not work alone or assist with medications before completing required training, and keep documentation.
Meet qualification criteria, deliver the content and give signed statements and rosters.
Complete required hours on time, maintain first aid, pass the medication exam if assisting with medications, and keep their certificates.
Provide time and resources for training.

documentation: Job descriptions and signed orientation acknowledgments
Training tracker and sign-in rosters
Certificates for first aid, dementia, postural supports, restricted conditions, hospice and medication assistance
Medication assistance exam results and written authorization to assist
Trainer qualification records and on-the-job trainer statements of content
Administrator certification and continuing education records

policies.title: Employee Health Screening and TB Screening
policies.applies_to: All personnel, including the licensee, administrator, direct care staff, kitchen, housekeeping and maintenance staff, and volunteers
federal: OSHA 29 CFR 1910.1030 (Bloodborne Pathogens Standard, where staff have occupational exposure)
policies.purpose: To make sure that every person who works in or is present at [AGENCY NAME] has been medically screened, including for tuberculosis, and is physically and emotionally able to be around residents. This protects residents and staff and meets the personnel health screening requirement of 22 CCR §87411.
policies.policy: [AGENCY NAME] requires a physician health screening for all personnel, including the licensee and administrator. The screening must include a chest x-ray or an intradermal (skin) test for tuberculosis. It must be completed no more than 6 months before, or no later than 7 days after, the date of employment or licensure. A signed physician report is required for each screening. It must state whether the person is physically qualified to perform the assigned duties and whether the person has any condition that would create a hazard to residents or other staff. Volunteers sign a statement of good health. Any staff member whose physical illness or emotional instability poses a significant threat to residents is relieved of duty. Health information is kept confidential and separate from the general personnel file contents where practical.

definitions.definition: A physician examination, with a chest x-ray or intradermal TB test, documented on a signed physician report (facility form LIC 503 or an equivalent report containing the required statements).
A TB skin test placed under the skin and read by a qualified health professional.
Every person who works in the facility as licensee, administrator, employee or contract worker, and anyone supervising residents or staff.
An unpaid person who assists the facility, is supervised, and is not counted in the staffing plan.

procedures: The administrator ([ADMINISTRATOR NAME]) gives every job applicant who receives a conditional offer the health screening form (LIC 503) and a written explanation of the screening requirement before the first day of work.
The applicant arranges the screening with a physician at the facility's expense or as stated in the offer letter. [AGENCY NAME] pays for the screening if required by California employment law.
The screening must be a physician examination that includes a chest x-ray or an intradermal TB test. The administrator confirms the form is signed by the physician.

The administrator checks the screening date. It must fall no more than 6 months before the start date or be completed within 7 days after the start date. A screening outside that window is not accepted and must be repeated.

The administrator reads the physician report to confirm it states whether the person is physically qualified for the duties and whether any condition creates a hazard. A report that is silent on either point is returned to the physician for completion.

If the person starts work before the screening is completed, the administrator enters a 7-day completion date on the new-hire checklist and does not allow the person to work after that date without a completed screening.

A person with a positive TB test, an abnormal chest x-ray, or reported symptoms of active TB is not assigned to resident care until a physician or the local health department states in writing that the person is not infectious.
The licensee and administrator complete the same screening and the screening report is kept in their own personnel records.
Each volunteer reads and signs a written statement of good health before beginning any volunteer activity. The administrator dates and files the statement.

The administrator keeps a personnel health screening tracking log listing each person, the screening date, the type of test, the result and any follow-up. The administrator reviews the log at least quarterly.
Any additional or repeat TB screening is done as directed by the person's physician, the local health officer or CDSS Licensing, and as required by the infection prevention plan (see SAF-07).
